In the absence of the Minister of Railways, the acting minister promised us some time ago that Mr. Maclean's report on freight rates would be brought down. Is the report ready ?
The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS ' AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair). There are two reports and they are now being printed. I hope to be able to bring them down perhaps some day next week.
The MINISTER OP JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved second reading of Bill (No. 19) respecting the Regina Law Library.
What is this Bill about ?

The law library at Regina was created by the government for the use of the judges of the North-west Territories. The territories have now sufficiently developed to have a Bar Association of their own. The intention of the Bill is to relieve the government of any further obligation with reference to the maintenance of that library and to hand it over to the Bar Association. This is done at the request of the association itself.
Are you going to get anything for the library ?

No. The library has been maintained up to the present at the expense of the government, and this Bill is passed with a view that it shall hereafter be maintained at the expense of the Law Association.
You take power for the Governor in Council to hand over the library absolutely upon such terms as they may see fit. I thought perhaps the terms include some payment.
It would be useless to do that, because, if we did maintain the library the Bar would have it for nothing. It is thought better to let the Bar have it and be done with it.

It would be foolish to try to get anything out of the lawyers at any rate.
Bill considered in committee, reported, read a third time and passed.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the House, and more particularly the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Customs to the law that we think is working most unfairly against the horse breeders of Manitoba and the North-west particularly, and also against the interest of the horse breeders throughout western Canada. I refer to the very low rate of the customs valuation at which horses are permitted to come into this country. The minimum value at which a horse may be imported is $15 and at the rate of 20 per cent the duty amounts only to the $3 which is practically nothing. In consequence a very inferior breed of horses has been admitted into the Northwest Territories and Manitoba. This practice has a most injurious effect upon the breed of horses. The horse breeders of Manitoba and the North-west Territories have gone to enormous expense in introducing from England, from Scotland, from Ireland and from the United States some of the very best blood to be procured in these countries. The effect has been to produce animals that are a credit to any country. But this has been seriously interfered with during the past few years by permitting cheap, low grade animals to come in at a valuation of ?15, or on payment of a duty of $3 per animal. The House will see the injurious effect that this must have on the breeding of horses in Canada. I understand that the evil has reached Ontario, and that car loads and even train loads of horses of this very inferior quality have been brought into that province during the last year or two.
Now, Sir, if there is anything that Canada is capable of producing within its own borders, it certainly is horses, because they will winter out in Manitoba and the North-west Territories and do exceedingly well. I think

it is only necessary to draw the attention of the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) to this matter to show him that it is really in the interest of the horse breeders and agriculturists of Canada that a stop should be put to this practice. Indian ponies, some of the most miserable scrubs to be found anywhere, are being imported, and nearly all the disease that has broken out in Manitoba and the North-west, such as glanders and a low kind of fever, has been traceable to these inferior animals. The Horse Breeders' Association of the Territories and the Horse Breeders' Association of Manitoba have passed very strong resolutions on this subject. I believe the general sentiment is that the valuation of imported horses should be increased to at least $75 or $100. A horse that is not worth that much should not be permitted to come into the country. Any man who has had any practical experience of horse breeding knows that he always falls short of producing what he expects and hopes for-that for every animal that comes up to his expectations there will be nine or ten that will fail to do so. So that we are always able to procure within our own bounds sufficient of the inferior grades of animals; and what we need is a larger number of the higher grade. Therefore, I trust that the government, having had an expression from those who are interested in this matter, not alone in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, but in Ontario, will see their way clear to meet their wishes by raising the valuation to a reasonable rate, which I think should be between $75 and $100.

Mr. Speaker, I have heard a great many complaints in Western Ontario' from those engaged in the breeding of horses and in farming operations about the evil which my hon. friend complains of. The introduction of this miserable class of cayuses, as they are termed-western ponies-which cost practically nothing, will have the effect of greatly deteriorating the quality of the stock in the country if it is not speedily put an end to. It is really a calamity to the agricultural classes of Canada that this trade is permitted, and I beg to ask the government to take the matter into their serious consideration. I think they will find, upon investigation, that it would be a public benefit to prevent the introduction of this class of horses into the country, either by the imposition of high duties or by some effective regulation. We have a good reputation for the character of the horses raised in Canada ; and, though that business has been to some degree depressed for a number of years past, it is again becoming a prosperous one. Our horses, especially our fast trotting and our carriage horses, are in good demand in the United States, and our farmers should be encouraged in the production of high grade animals. I can only
add my protest to that of the hon. member who has spoken as to the impropriety of permitting this trade in cayuses to continue.

Mr. Speaker, in support of the case which has been presented by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), I do not know that I can do better than read to the House an extract from the last report of the Commissioner of Agriculture for the Territories, which is as follows
Although the territories, particularly the western portion thereof, are plentifully supplied with native horses of a very low standard of excellence, for which it is practically an impossibility to find a market, the importation of scrub horses is still going on, thus materially aggravating the unfavourable market conditions for the above mentioned class of horses. The United States supplied us with some 6,000 horses during the past year at an average value per head of about $20. Representations have in the past been made to the Dominion government by agricultural societies in the territories, the Western Stock Growers' Association and the Horse Breeders' Association of Manitoba with a view to having the valuation of horses brought in from the United States placed on a reasonable basis. At the present time the minimum valuation is placed at $15. It would appear that no hardship would be inflicted upon dealers and purchasers if this amount were raised to $40 or $50. It may safely be taken for granted that any horse worth less than $50 is not required in this country, either for breeding purposes or for actual use.
I may say that it is not from the point of view of a protectionist in the ordinary tariff sense that I support the plea of my hon. friend. We ask that the change be made for the purpose of protecting the country from the importation of an undesirable class of horses. Nor do the Horse Breeders' Association make the request in the usual protectionist spirit. In a document issued some time ago by that Association, I find the following, written by the secretary. After stating the matter, he goes on to say :
In submitting the above I am directed by my Executive Committee to point out as emphatically as lies in my power, that the object territorial horse breeders have in view in agitating for the imposition of a minimum valuation on importations of horses, somewhat in keeping with the necessities of the case, is not to secure the benefits of a protective tariff, which such a restriction would naturally amount to were the supply of horses now in the west insufficient to fill the local requirements and the value inflated. What the territorial breeders particularly ask protection against is the importation of inferior stock, which must inevitably lower the standard of horses in this country, already much too low, and consequently the reputation of the territories as a horse producing country.
The idea which I think should prevail in this matter is something similar to that which prevails in regard to the importation of pernicious literature. I do not know

that I would wish to go farther than the association; I do not know that I would wish to goi as far as my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), who asks that the valuation be raised to $75 or $100. At the last meeting of the association held in Calgary, a little less than a year ago, a motion was proposed to ask the government to make the valuation $40. An amendment was submitted asking that the valuation be made $35, and an amendment to the amendment was proposed and adopted asking for the fixing of the amount at $50. That is what the association asks, and that is as far as I would ask the government to go.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is pretty good protection.

That would, I think, fairly and satisfactorily protect the country from animals which may be termed ' scrubs.' I might quote further from a letter which I received from the secretary of the association :
Our members, who represent every portion of the west, have no desire for protection, as the word is generally applied.
The general idea of urging upon the authorities to have the change in question made is, that in the opinion of the association, horses worth less than $50 each, are not required in this country either for breeding purposes or for actual use.
I hope the government will find that a clear enough case has been made out to warrant their acceding to the request of tha association.

I am glad this matter has been brought up as I myself had intended to. call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to it. I am personally convinced that there is a great deal of need for raising the valuation of horses brought into this country. There is no doubt that there is considerable disease among the poorer class of horses now brought in from the other side of the line, and some steps should be taken to put a stop to the evil. Dealers bring those small horses in droves north through Alberta up towards Edmonton, selling as they go, and spreading them over the country. I have here the report of Mr. Perry, Commissioner of the North-west Mounted Police, from which I take the following :
There is one subject that demands attention, and that is the importation of a worthless class of horses, half-breeds and Indians. They go south of the line and acquire a certain number of ponies which they smuggle into the territories. Apart from these being an undesirable class of animal, they are not inspected by sny veterinary surgeon, and as a consequence the glanders or other infectious or contagious diseases can be introduced.
It would appear further that even when the smugglers referred to in this report
are caught, they are not punished and thus .are encouraged to carry on their nefarious traffic. Here is what Mr. Perry says on this point:
During the past years several seizures of such stock have been made, and in every case the owners have be m allowed to regain possession of their horses on paying duty and expenses. In one case where the horses had been brought in by half-breeds some had actually teen sold, still they were allowed to pay the duty and go scot free. Until more severe measures are taken Indians and half-breeds will continue to smuggle in horses and take their chances of being canght. If they are caught, it means just paying duty and if not caught they are that much ahead.
These worthless horses range the southern country in large numbers, and but little attention is paid to disease among them. They are extensively smuggled across, and disease is thus spread broadcast throughout our country. I hope that the Ministers of Agriculture and Customs will do something to put a stop to this evil.

1 wish we could invent some word that would mean protection, ns we all want it, and yet would not spell it, because every man in this country wants protection, but a great many want it under some other name. Some want it so that they may be on equal terms with their opponents, but disclaim the word 'protection.' I heard a ship builder say : We want to be put on as favourable terms as our opponents so that they will not be able to sell ships cheaper to Canada than we can build them for. Our hon. friends in the west disclaim wanting protection, but they want a horse which is worth $5 in the states valued at $50 here, and have the duty charged on that extra value. But, of course, they don't want protection. Well, it is a protection that will suit us.
Make it $100.

That would be better and carry out protection to its full extent. 1 speak as a western man, interested for many years in horse breeding in the Northwest, in which business unfortunately I have lost a good many hundreds and thousands of dollars. We imported high class animals from Scotland, and for fifteen or more years have been breeding stock, and our experience is that the low grade stock which comes into the North-west competes with our high grade stock. In connection with my own ease, we suffered to such an extent from that competition that we went out of business last year. As an instance of the extent of that competition I may mention that near Edmonton, three years ago, I saw a band of least 500 horses which had been driven across from Wyoming, about a thousand miles distant. Those horses were being sold, from the boundary up to Edmonton, as low, some of them, as $5 a head. It would have been

better for Canada to have paid the value of these horses and shot them as they crossed the border. It is a great temptation to the farmers, who have great difficulty in getting ready money, to buy horses at $10 or $20 a piece, although in a few years time they realize that they have done themselves great injury. If a farmer can get a horse for $10 or $20, he is strongly tempted to buy it, trusting that no matter how poor and miserable it is, it will be able to do the work for a year or two. It is a great pity that the government should allow that class of horses to come into the country. I do not know whether they are inspected as they come over the border or not, but there is no doubt that the evil effects of allowing such poor stock to come in will be felt twenty years hence, and the thanks of the House are due to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. (Boyd) 'for having brought this matter to our attention.

The amusing candor of the hon. members representing the North-west Territories is shown in the fact that they are so exceedingly anxious to have the lowest possible duty on agricultural implements and things pertaining thereto, but the highest possible duty on horses and other animals that are raised there. It shows the insincerity of the protectionist, who changes his attitude according to the interest he considers.
Mr. LaRIVIBRE. We raise horses, but we do not make agricultural implements.

I happen to represent a county in the province of Ontario that claims to raise the best horses in the Dominion, and I have not heard from the consumers of horses, if I may use the term, any special protest against these American horses coming in, the number which is comparatively small. I think that if a party wants to buy a cheap horse, he ought to be allowed to do so. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) gives away the whole case in the admission he makes that the introduction of these horses to the Northwest is a serious temptation to the farmer there. The farmer is struggling against the difficulties that he encounters in the Northwest, and it may be that he feels like buying a low-price horse. Of course, you do not put on a duty to increase the price, but you put some sort of hindrance in his way, so that this farmer struggling in adversity may not buy the cheap horse, but will be compelled to buy the higher-priced animal. The moment you admit the spirit of paternalism you cannot deal with one interest alone, but must consider the effect upon industry generally. It seems to me that the '' ise course is, while we have regard to Canadian interests as far as possible-and I am glad to see the development of all Canadian interests-to leave this industry as free from embarrassing conditions as possible.

There is a great tendency in the House to run from special cases to generalities. It is impossible to bring up any question, let it be great or small, but forthwith the general politics of the country must be tagged on to it on one side or the other. This question of a proposed minimum valuation of horses certainly has two sides. It is brought up by those who are interested in breeding horses, as distinguished from those who are using horses. It is a question for the House to consider whether the interests of the country at large are to be best served by conforming to the idea of the rearer of horses or of the user of horses. We cannot be on both sides-at least all of us cannot be on both sides of every question all the time.
Oh, yes.

Speak for yourselves, please. We cannot be on both sides of this question at once, but must take sides either with the rearers of horses or the users of horses. Now, as representing probably the largest and most populous agricultural constituency in this Dominion, I have no hesitation on this occasion, in taking sides with the rearers of horses as against the users of inferior horses. Hon. gentlemen who have seen fit to tag on an argument of free trade or protection to this question, who think they have rather struck oil in making an attack on those who are attempting to forward a particular interest of this great country, let me suggest that, while we ask that a minimum valuation be placed upon horses, we are not only willing but we are anxious that horses above a certain valuation shall be admitted free. I think every horse rearer in the country will agree to that proposition. Those who framed the tariff which is in force at the present time saw fit to admit certain valuable horses free, and everybody who is interested in the horse business in this country, agrees that that is a sound business proposition. Then, just as it is reasonable and desirable to admit certain superior classes of horses free of duty into this country, it is reasonable and desirable to exclude, as far as possible, certain inferior classes of horses from this country. Every practical agriculturist thoroughly understands that a good horse is good for the country and a poor horse is bad for the country. The less we have of the poorer class of horses the better. If we are going to great expense, as we are in all parts of the country, individually, municipally, provincially and nationally, to improve our stock of horses; and if we recognize, as we do, the great necessity of that improvement to the highest degree all over the country, then I ask hon. gentlemen, is it common sense to leave the bars down, to allow these efforts that we are making to improve our horses to be destroyed by the influx of an undesirable class of horses ? It

lias been pointed out that it is this class of horses of low valuation, which, because they are of low valuation do not receive the attention that is given to horses of greater value, that are really the cause of the introduction of diseases of various kinds into our country. These are the horses which frustrate the efforts which we are making to improve our stock both directly and indirectly. I repeat, it is not a question of improving the horse stock of this country by a simple manipulation of the tariff; it is a question of taking such means as may be reasonable and as are necessary to prevent the deterioration of our horse stock by certain means within our knowledge under our control. The suggestion is made that one way of doing this would be to place a minimum valuation on horses brought in from the United States. Any other means that will gain the same end will be entirely acceptable. If any better means can be suggested by any hon, member, I am safe in saying that those who are interested will be glad to accept them. We are not particularly anxious that the improvement shall be brought about by a minimum valuation. That seems a ready and easy means of arriving at this necessary result, to save the pasture of our prairie for valuable stock, to conserve the efforts we are making to improve our horses, to place the horse-raising industry of this country upon the highest level of the whole world, which is what we ought to endeavour to achieve, and what we can achieve, I believe, if reasonable measures are taken. It is quite possible that the country may prosper, and that the horse industry may prosper, whether the present minimum valuation increased or .not. But we take the liberty of placing before this House of Commons the facts of the case as practical men, representing a practical question, and we ask for practical action by the House with regard to mere theories.

I l-ise to express my sympathy with the efforts that our western friends are putting forth to increase the quality of the Canadian horse. I do not object at all to the attitude they have taken. I believe the precautions that they desire are in the interests of the country. I rise for the purpose of drawing to the attention of the House an exactly similar state of affairs that happens to exist in Ontario. Last week the carriage makers of the Dominion of Canada came down here in a very strong deputation representing nearly $5,000,000 in capital, and they told the government that they were being subjected to unfair competition from the United States. They said, with the excellency of our work we have completely captured the Canadian carriage, cutter and buggy trade. The importations from the outside world are only $39,000 worth, only enough carriages to employ 25 men in their production. We can compete against the United States
in their own market, we are willing to put down the bars and let American carriages come in if they will take down the bars and let Canadian carriages go in. We can beat them in neutral markets, we can beat them in their own markets, we can beat them in Canadian markets, because we make a first-class carriage, out of the best material, of the best workmanship, and durable to a high degree. But what troubles us now is, not the importation of a high grade of American carriages, or horses, as our friends from the west might say, but an inferior class of slop work that is being made in the United States, where a factory in Michigan is turning out about 70,000 carriages per annum, made from the refuse of other factories, against which the Canadian manufacturer cannot compete. We say therefore, as our friends say, that we don't want you to raise the duty. The duty is high enough. We can fight against fair competition, but we cannot compete against the scrub horses or shoddy carriages. What we want you to do is to raise the minimum price of a carriage to $50, just as these gentlemen want the minimum price of a horse raised to $50 to keep out the scrub horses. Keep out this American slop work, and allow Canadians to have first-class carriages. Now, we are anxious to keep up the high quality of our horses in Canada. So are we also anxious to keep up the quality of our carriages, so that when a gentleman takes his lady out, or when a more reverend senior goes to church, he can travel in safety without fear of breaking down through being the owner of a slop made buggy. I approve the efforts our friends are making, I hope the government will listen to their request, and that when they raise the scale of horses to $50, they will also raise the scale of scrub carriages to $50.

I hope the House will not think we are all protectionists in the North-west Territories because several hon. gentlemen from that country have advocated the raising of the valuation of a horse coming in from the other side of the line. One of the arguments used has been that we want to improve the stock. I do not understand how raising the valuation of a horse from $15 to $50 is going to have any effect in improving the stock in the North-west Territories, more particularly as we have thousands of the very same class of horses running all over the plains, belonging to the Blood Indians and other tribes. So I do not think that is any argument. Now, with reference to the horses that are coming in. I understand the Territorial Horse Breeders' Association have passed resolutions, which they have sent to every member from the North-west Territories, asking to have the valuation raised. My hon. friend from Toronto, who a moment ago said that he was interested in the horse raising business up there, admitted that there was a certain amount of benefit to the poorer clas-

ses of the community in the North-west by letting these same horses come in at the price they were coming in to-day. He said that farmers going in without much money would be able to buy a cheap team of horses. We know that we are getting into that country at the present time a good class of settlers, and I am pleased to say a great many of them are a better class of people, and are bringing in a better class of horses with them. Still there are parties coming in that cannot afford to buy expensive horses ; and if they need to be able to buy a cheap team of horses to do their work, I think they should be considered just as much as the Territorial Horse Breeders' Association, or the ranchers. [DOT]
Can you break sod with one of these ?

Yes. If you cannot break sod with one of them, you can break sod with three of them, if not with three, with four. Then again, as has been pointed out, you want horses for other purposes besides breaking sod. We have creameries in the North-west Territories, and people who live at a distance from them and who want to take their cream to a factory, cannot take a team of heavy Clydesdales for that purpose ; they have to have driving horses, and they get these horses very cheap. I think the government should make haste slowly in raising the valuation, of horses, more particularly as I do not see that it is going to have the effect of improving the stock in the Territories, inasmuch as we have the same class of horses up there ourselves. It is a well known fact that in Alberta to-day you can buy horses for $3 a piece, and they are not imported from the United States, they are raised by Indians up there. I may say it would not be a bad thing if the Indian Department were to take some action with reference to horses running round through the west, belonging to the Indians. It would have a better effect than raising the valuation of the few horses that are brought in from the United States.
Now, with reference to the remarks of my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd). I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to go into a budget debate, or to deal with questions outside the one that is before the Chair. But I must say that when my hon. friend talks about a duty on buggies and that sort of thing, I want him to understand that so far as I am concerned, I have not gone back on the faith at ail. We do not manufacture anything at all in the North-west Territories, we have to buy our produce from the outside, and we get no benefit from protection at all ; though we are quite willing to bear our share of the heat and burden of the day and to pay a reasonable amount so long as it is a duty for revenue. But when any person commences to talk about imposing taxes, or doing anything else for the purpose of protecting any industry, Mr. DAVIS.
whether a horse industry, or a cow industry, or any other industry, then I shall certainly oppose it at every opportunity.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) There is one view of this subject that I think is entirely wrong, and that is to place a fictitious value upon anything coming into this country, greater than the article has in the country from which it is exported. I think that principle is wrong from the very outset. I would suggest that those who want to keep these scrub horses out of the Dominion should adopt the American tariff, because no horses are admitted into the United States, so far as I can ascertain, at less than 30 per cent. If you put a specific duty on these horses you would get clear of the trouble.

Mr. Speaker, as a producer of horses in the province of Ontario, I may say that the farmers in my part of the country feel very keenly the injury that is being inflicted upon them by the importation of scrub horses from the United States. These horses are taking the place of our own horses and greatly lessening the demand for good horses. You can get these imported horses in droves, yet, the hon. gentleman who spoke last tried to make out that the people of Canada wanted to import horses from the United States although there are thousands of Canadian horses running on the prairies of the west. These inferior horses, which are brought into the country and which are useless for all ordinary purposes, displace a great many of our own animals. On the same principle as those who are asking for protection in horses and carriages, we, as farmers, want a tax put on corn, because the free corn imported from the United States displaces a great deal of our Ontario coarse grains. When they want protection for their horses, we want protection for our grain, and I do not care whether they call it tariff, or whether they put a fraudulent valuation on their horses ; as long as they put a high duty on these scrub horses it will satisfy the farmers in Ontario. If the western people are not satisfied with the tariff let them put a fraudulent value on then- horses and let the duty be collected accordingly. I am very much pleased that this important question has been brought to the attention of the hon. members of this House. I think, without taking politics into consideration at all, that it will be only fair on the part of the government to impose a higher tariff on the horses which are shipped across the line and which are selling in towns all over the country all the way from $11 up to $30, and which are taking the places of home bred horses that we have gone to such expense to produce. I am glad to hear hon. members of this House calling for protection. or fraudulent valuation, I care not which it may be.
Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to say a word
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) has already spoken.
I think it is in order that some harness maker should speak. We have the horse and buggy but we have no harness.

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC' WORKS (Hon. J. Israel Tarte). The chief engineer tells me that it will be at the foot of Bay-Held street, although I am not quite sure. We have not carried out the work so far because we have no deed of the wharf property. This is a new one.

Motion agreed to.
["I move that the word be ' construction ' instead of ' reconstruction and repairs.'"]
You have fixed the place where the wharf is to be built ?
Yes.

It is to be in the
place the hon. minister says ?

Yes.
Bayfield-extension of south pier, $3,600.
This work is under contract and this sum is to complete the work.
Who recommended this expenditure in the first place ?
It was, I think, the late lamented Mr. McMillan. The work is under contract, the contractor being Mr. Clark, of Goderich.
Is that the total cost ?
The total cost.
Is this work approved by the present representative of South Huron (Mr. McEwen) ?
I did not ask his approval. I had no need to do it because the work was under contract.

I would like to know whether the hon. member for South Huron approves of this work. It seems to me that it is an unnecessary work and a useless waste of money. I can see no object in spending this sum of money at Bayfield at all. Perhaps the hon. member for South Huron could give us some information.

This work is now under contract. It is a work that has been in existence for years and one on which the late administration have spent over $70,000. There is nothing new in it. We are simply extending and repairing an old work.

Years ago, when money was expended on Bayfield harbour, it was really necessary to have a harbour there, but the hon. gentleman has not discovered that the circumstances have changed since then, and I would like to know what use will be made of this harbour. Would boats come in there, or is there a railway that runs to that place ? Is it for the accommodation of a few fishing boats ? I doubt very much whether there are any fishing boats at that port.

I never knew that it was necessary to have a railway running to a wharf to make a work of this kind necessary. Very far from it. When there is no railway people are more in need of harbour accommodation.
What about the boats ?
I do not own any boat there.

Bayfield has been a port for a considerable length of time," and the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) knows it as well as I do. There is not a great deal of shipping done there now but there is a great deal of fishing, and boats call there just the same.
I would like to hear from the hon. gentleman for South Huron who is well posted as to this work, and he knows that what I say is perfectly true.

What does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) want ? This work was constructed years ago and it cost the late government $70,000. I am not going to remove that work, am I ? This vote is simply to keep it in repair and to extend it a little.

I will tell the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) what I want. We have a large number of public works in this country on which it is necessary to expend public money, and there are other works on which public money was expended in the past because it was necessary to do so, but on which it is not necessary to expend any more money. In the case of this harbour circumstances have changed, and it is not



necessary now to spend public money on it. What good is there to be gained if there are no boats going to the harbour. It is simply a useless waste of money. Does it follow because a useless expenditure of money has been made one year, that the government is going to continue that useless expenditure for ever. I say we should call a halt in cases like this. I am in favour of spending public money on public works which are necessary, but when it is shown that public works are not necessary I am [DOT]opposed to spending money on them.

I cannot believe that the late government would have spent $70,000 on this work if there was no use for it. Last year I was authorized by this parliament to let the contract and the money was voted. I think objection should have been taken then.

Last year this item escaped without any discussion, but inquiries have since shown that this is a useless waste of money and I would be negligent in my duty if I did not draw attention to it.
I agree with the minister that the expenditure of $70,000 in days gone by was justifiable, but the time has now arrived when a further expenditure on that harbour is mot justifiable.

If lion, gentlemen on the "other side object to this work they should Kave done so last year when the vote was taken. This is not the time to raise a row about this small item. The money was voted last year and the contract let, and this is simply a revote. It is true that money was expended on this harbour years ago, but it must be' remembered that large boats called there and that not so long ago either. I remember that the 1 Asia ' and ' Sovereign ' used to call there some years ago, and there is no good reason why when that harbour is finished large steamers will not call there again. Bayfield has no railway and there is consequently all the more necessity for boats calling there. Besides that fact, there is a large number of fishermen at Bayfield, We see that in the lower provinces they build harbours for their fishing fleets, and there is no good reason why Bayfield should not have the same treatment. During the Conservative regime the harbour was allowed to get out of repair ; the sand drifted across a break, and the fishermen could not get in or out. This was not fair. The late government spent money on that harbour on two occasions and the work was swept away. The work done by the present government remains there and is in good shape and what money is being expended now will make the harbour useful.
It is curious to know the guiding principle of the Minister of Public Works in these expenditures. The hon. gentleman has told us frankly that the late government spent $70,000 on the harbour

and that they would not do so if it was not a useful expenditure. It is pertinent to ask the Minister of Public Works now if he ever uses his own judgment. Has he any knowledge of the present utility of the work. He is not asking money for repairs but to make an extension of an old work and he should produce some report from his engineers as to the necessity for this new work.

It was represented to me by the late Mr. McMillan, the respected member for that riding, whom we are all sorry is not sitting in his seat in this House-that this was a work of some importance. I find from the records that the late government were so impressed with this, that they bought that work from private owners and spent $70,000 on it. Before reaching a conclusion on this matter I naturally asked for a report from Major Gray, the resident engineer, and in his repoi't dated 27th of April, 1900, he states that he consulted several vessel men of the port with regard to the extension of the pier and they were all of opinion, that the north pier running so much in a southerly direction nearly closes the mouth of the harbour, and that if vessels by any chance miss the southern pier they are at once on shore. Major Gray states that he has himself seen two vessels ashore on that account. It was reported to me officially by an able engineer that the extension of one of the piers was necessary to protect life and property. I do not understand why my hon. friends on the other side from Ontario, object so much to a work for which their own government paid $70,000, and which I am only improving. I cannot understand the position they take unless of course they are acting as they have a right to do-well for political motives, which is not after all very wrong. However, the country will judge of the facts. Here was a work on which $70,000 had been spent by our predecessors, having been bought from private owners, and I cannot understand why there is so much opposition to this vote, especially when a sum of money was voted last year.
When was the last public money spent on this wharf ?
I have not all the dates here.

Perhaps I can give the House the explanation of the matter. This work is in a constituency which I once had the honour to represent, and I recollect tolerably well the circumstances under which, even when I was in opposition, and when I was not much of a favourite of the government, the late government did spend some money there. The coast of Lake Huron, as most hon. gentlemen who have ever crossed that lake know, is an exceedingly dangerous coast, and very scantily provided with harbours. I think that from Goderich to

Sarnia there are hardly any natural harbours. The consequence is that any vessels, small or large, that miss. Goderich in a gale, find it very difficult to get any shelter. The late government thought that it was desirable to establish a small harbour of refuge at Bayfield. That was the reason they gave for the expenditure they entered into. That harbour had, I think, very little trade proper, but it was supposed by the late government, and also by the vessel owners of Goderich, to be of use as a harbour of refuge under certain conditions. The sum demanded by my hon. friend, $3,600, for the extension of the south pier is, I understand, to ensure the harbour being useful for the purpose for which the original expenditure was incurred. These are the circumstances, and they appear to perfectly justify my hon. friend in asking for this vote.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: If the water were deep enough and it were possible for vessels in distress to go into the harbour, there would be some justification for the argument of the hon. gentleman; but there is not a sufficient depth of water, even with the extension of the pier, and that is why I say that this is a useless expenditure. The hon. gentleman knows very well the vessel trade to-day at this point is very different to what it was years ago, when the pier was first built. At that time there were a large number of small vessels, but there are very few to-day.

Perhaps I might read a word or two from the debate which took place when this matter was up in 1891. Here is what was said by Mr. Cameron, who then represented that county :
The hon. gentleman knows that $50,000 has been expended by the government at Bayfield, and I tell him that money has been practically thrown away.
If the expenditure was wrong under the late government, surely at this advanced time it cannot be proper not only to repair the wharf, but to extend it. Perhaps the minister will be good enough to say what is the population of that place to-day, as compared with ten years ago ?
I really cannot say what the population is.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is wrong in saying that Mr. Cameron represented that constituency at that time. He did not represent it in 1891.
Yes, he did.

Well, I will accept that. Bayfield is a small incorporated village. It is true, the trade of the place is not very large, but I think it is necessary that a certain amount of money should be spent there in order to retain the work already done. To dredge out the harbour and make 39i
it an absolutely safe harbour of refuge would require the expenditure of several thousand dollars. The money now being spent will, I understand, make it a harbour of refuge for smaller vessels. During the last few years the place has come into prominence as a summer resort, and even many Americans come there.

The reason this harbour went out of use was because it was out of repair for a number of years, the lake having washed away a part of the pier and covered it with sand. For this reason the vessels could not get in, and the trade fell off. The present government has repaired the pier, and it is now fit for vessels to come in, and consequently the trade will come back.
Did I understand the hon. member for West Huron to say that the population was now about 1,000 ?
No, I said the place was an incorporated village, which I understood required 1,000 to be incorporated. I do not know what the population is now.
The hon. gentleman lives within a few miles of the place. What is its population V
I suppose the population is 800 or 900.
The fact is that its population is less than it was ten years ago It stands now at 559.
That is not the fault of the wharf.
Does the minister intend to dredge this harbour this year ?

I do not think we have yet made up our minds to dredge it. I will look into the question carefully, to see whether it is necessary to have dredging done; but to-day I am only applying for money to extend the pier.

But the hon. gentleman must see that it is a useless expenditure of money, because even with the extension of the pier the water is not deep enough. If the hon. gentleman is expending the money for the purpose of benefiting the fishermen, half this sum is sufficient, because it would not be necessary to extend the pier, but only to repair it. But, outside of that, this expenditure is a pure waste of money.
Who has charge of this work, superintending it ?

Mr. Jonas Marks, who has been recommended by my hon. friend, will have charge of the work.
Blind river-wharf, $6,o00.
Where is this Blind river ?

On the north channel of the lake leading to Georgian Bay. It is in the district of Algoma, on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is a lumbering village, situated eight miles west of Algoma, and about eighty miles east of Sault Ste. Marie. The business consists principaly of lumbering. There are two large mills. This is a very thriving farming community. The population at the last census was 600. We have chosen a site, but the deeds are not yet in our possession. The plans are ready and tenders will be called for.
What will be the total cost ?
Eleven thousand dollars.

How much for the site ?
The MINISTER OF PuBLIC WORKS. We have not purchased a site yet, and that is why we have not asked for tenders.
I may be misinformed, but I understand that this is purely a wharf for some American lumbering company who have mills there-that it is solely for their convenience.

My hon. friend the exMinister of Railways has been altogether misinformed. Some years ago there was an old wharf in use there by the Blind River Lumber Company, but that company went out of existence and a new American concern bought out the property, and fitted up this old wharf for their own use. They will not allow other people's boats to tie up at it. Their refusal to allow steamboats* from Owen Sound and Collingwood to tie up there obliges the merchants to have their goods landed at Algoma Mills, some seven or eight miles east of Blind river, and thence tranship them at considerable expense by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is a very good agricultural and farming country back of Blind river-one of the many places in my county which have a very bright future indeed. I can assure the House that this work iS absolutely necessary.
Why did not private individuals build the wharf ?
I do not know that there is anybody there really able to build it.
On whose property is the money to be expended ?
A site is being selected but not bought. There are two sites, and we have chosen one.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: From whom ?

We have not bought it yet. We have made our choice, as far as the engineer is con-Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
cerned. We approve that site because it is one on which the work will cost the least.

It might be fitting for me to call attention to an expenditure that appears on page Y-218 of the Auditor General's Report relating to the Sarnia dredging. I asked the hon. gentleman to lay the progress estimates, the advertisements for tenders, and the tenders themselves, on the Table. Can the hon. gentleman now give me the information ? In the meantime, I would like to ask him what the nature of that work is, who owns the dredging plant, if the property on which the work is being done is private property or belongs to the government, the extent of the work, and if the sum expended exceeds the amount first contemplated ?

When my hon. friend spoke jmvately to me, I thought he was referring to the dredging done at Point Edward, but I see now that I did not understand him. My engineer informs me that the work to which he alludes was let by public tender to Mr. O'Leary, and is completed. It was a piece of dredging which was given two years ago. I was away when that piece of work was given out. When my hon. friend spoke to me a day or two ago, I thought he was alluding to the new work carried out at Point Edward. If he wants more information, as to the particular work he now asks about, I will bring it down with pleasure. I will bring down the whole cost.
Did the hon. gentleman make any inquiry as to whether the work was done on private property or on property which belongs to the government ?
My chief engineer says that the dredging was done in the channel of the river, as far as he can remember. He will take note of what my hon. friend wants and furnish the information required.

Another thing I would like him to take note of is this : My information is that this work was done entirely on the property of some American mill owners. I am not finding fault because they are Americans, for we all welcome American capital as we do any other capital, but the minister would be entirely without justification in spending public money on private property. My information is that it has been spent entirely on private property, and that the owners of the property were doing the work with their own dredges-American dredges and American workmen-when Mr. O'Leary stepped in to be rewarded for party services and got the contract and used the dredge belonging to an American company. The dredge is owned by the mill owners who were doing the work themselves before the hon. gentleman stepped in to give Mr. O'Leary some little solace for his disappointment in not getting a certain office. Perhaps

the hon. gentleman can explain whether the plant belongs to Mr. O'Leary, and if not, to whom ? Also, whether the dredging was not being done before by the mill owners, in whose interests this work is being done now ?

I can only repeat what I said a minute ago. The work was given by public tender to Mr. O'Leary, who was the successful tenderer. As to whether the dredge was an American dredge or not, I cannot say now.
I was not in the country when that work was awarded. I shall inquire and give the hon. gentleman the information he desires. Perhaps I may be allowed to state that on two or three occasions, if not more, during last year, I was obliged to have recourse to American dredges, because I could not secure Canadian ones. The question was whether an elevator was to be built on Canadian soil or American soil at Port Huron, and we had to make up our minds pretty quick. The Grand Trunk people came to see me, and also the interested parties. The member for the riding represented that the elevator was to be located on the American side unless we did the dredging. WTe could not secure a Canadian dredge for love or money, so I engaged an American dredge.
I suppose the hon. minister is not giving this as a justification in the case I referred to.
In that case, I was not here, and knew nothing about it personally.
I hope the hon. gentleman will inform himself and give us the facts later on.
With pleasure.
Is the work in the River Sydenham completed ? There is no item in the estimate this year. How much of the vote of last year was expended 1
If the hon. gentleman will repeat his question when the items for dredging are before us I shall be glad to give him information.
I understood the minister to say that a site had been selected at Blind river, but not purchased. On whose recommendation was it selected, and who owns the property ?
It was selected on the recommendation of the chief engineer.
What was the price ?
The estimate placed upon the site by the engineer is $250.
Does the minister select the site and afterwards fix a price ?

We make a survey with a view to choosing a site, and when we have ascertained the best site, we try to buy it. What else can we do ? We have confidential reports from the engineer, and we do not make public where we wish to buy.
Who owns the property selected ?

I really do not remember.
Bronte-harbour improvements, $3,000.

Last year $7,000 was voted for this work. Would the minister please state how much of that has been expended, also whether this $3,000 now asked for is likely to complete the work. I might say that it is very desirable that this work should be completed-not only the docks but the dredging. The people are hoping for this, and they expect it. I trust the work will be fully completed during the coming summer.

Out of tlie $7,000 voted last session, $6,209 was spent. The balance will be spent as soon as the season opens. I am glad to say that the $3,000 that I am now asking for will complete the work, and the work will be finished during the present year.
Burlington channel-repairs to pier, $50,000.
There was a large vote for this purpose last year. How much of it was expended.

We did not spend very much, because the contractor has only been gathering materials, so far, and has not done much work. We have not given the estimates. The amount spent up to the 15th of December was $1,122.
That would be for material, I suppose.
Yes.
On which side of the channel is the work to be done ? Is the entire pier to be rebuilt ?
We are rebuilding the pier on the south side. At first we were not very successful, and had to take the work from the contractor. We are renovating the pier, making it 991 feet long.
What is the amount of the contract ?
Are there to be any repairs on the north side of the channel ?
No.
Will this complete the work ?
Yes.
What time has the contractor for the completion of the work ?
The contract is to be completed on the 10th of April, 1903. Practically, this means that it will have to be completed next fall.
Who has the contract ?

James Clarke, of Goderich, the lowest tenderer.
Collingwood-harbour improvements, $40,000.

The minister will please give us a full statement of the expenditure there, the depth of water in the harbour, the time when he expects to complete the work and the estimated total cost. I suppose he has had some marine surveyors to survey the channel and will be able to give us all necessary information. I do not object to an expenditure on Collingwood. I think that, perhaps, it is one of the harbours on the lakes that ought to be made a good harbour. When I was in office there was a report in the marine department from Commander Bolton, who had made a survey of the Georgian Bay, and who reported that it would be almost impossible to make a harbour out of Collingwood. He gave a detail of the harbour and his reasons for the conclusions he had reached. What is the width of the channel that the hon. minister is making leading into the harbour
We have dredged a channel 110 feet wide, giving a depth of 20 feet for the whole length from open water to the inside harbour.
What is the length of the trench, or whatever you call it ?
The length of channel that we have dredged so far is 2,350 feet.
To complete it, how much will it require ?

We want to give it a width of 110 feet and a length of 200 feet. The mouth of that channel is not wide enough. My hon. friend knows that Collingwood, since we have given it that accommodation, has grown a good deal. There is a large ship Hon. Mr. TARTE.
yard in which two large ships have already been built; a large saw-mill has been erected during the last year or two, there is a large packing factory, in fact, Collingwood is one of the most thriving towns on the Georgian Bay. Collingwood, Midland, Owen Sound, Meaford, all these towns are getting along very nicely indeed. The width of the channel is not sufficient, because boats navigating those waters are being built of a larger size constantly. A large trade is being done there, and it will be necessary to enlarge that channel. But we do not intend to do a large amount of additional work all at once. This money is especially to enlarge the entrance to the harbour. I have heard about the same statement that my hon. friend has heard, namely, that Collingwood is a difficult port to make. But the fact that there is already a large fleet of steamers visiting that port proves that after all it is not so bad as other ports. I am sorry to add that perhaps there is a little jealousy among certain harbours. But there is no reason for jealousy, because there is trade for them all.

If that be correct, I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that some few years ago an application was made from Port Credit for an expenditure of money to repair and keep up the present pier and dock. At that time it was not definitely promised, but the minister promised the deputation, or the hon. gentleman representing the county at the time, that he would give it his favourable consideration. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could now tell the House, as he has already stated there is plenty for all, that we will come in under that general term.
I must say that the word ' all ' does not cover what my hon. friend has just suggested. I do not remember at all the fact he has referred to about Port Credit.

No doubt the hon. gentleman remembered it pretty well a few years ago, when that county chanced to be represented by an hon. member who supported the present government. He tells us that this harbour does not come under the designation of ' all.' I assume it is because circumstances have changed, and that the county, instead of being represented by a supporter of the government, as it was at the time the deputation waited upon the Minister of Public Works, is now represented by an hon. member sitting on the side of the opposition. I listened to the remarks of the Minister of Public Works, and it certainly struck me in his definite statement that this harbour did not come under the designation that he referred to, and that he intends to perpetuate the policy of assisting only those counties that give the government support. That seems to be the fixed policy of the government; otherwise I think the hon. gentleman would

meet the wishes of mj hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) as faiily as he promised he would meet the wishes of the former representative of that riding. .

I did not intend in my remarks to convey any such meaning as my hon. friend gathered from them. What I meant to say by the word ' all ' was that I did not remember the harbour to which my hon. friend referred. The best evidence that I am not as wicked as my hon. friend thinks, is* that I am at this moment carrying on a public work in his own riding.
There is the council, I have no right to go ahead of my colleagues.

I have not said that I would never pay any attention to Port Credit. During the last two days I hffve received I suppose 25 or 30 petitions for work that I have not been able to accede to, and my hon. friend must not be surprised if, on the spur of the moment, I am not prepared to say that I will do any work at Port Credit.
Perhaps the hon. minister will promise the House to put something in the supplementary estimates.

My hon. friend has as good as a promise from the Minister of Public Works that the matter is under his consideration, and probably there will be an item in the supplementary estimates for him. However, in reference to Collingwood harbour, if I understand the minister aright, he intends to expend this $40,000 which he is asking us for now, to widen the prism from 110 to 200 feet. A great part of it is for that purpose. I quite concede the necessity of the work. Fancy a vessel coming into the port of Collingwood with a side wind, passing down 2,300 feet, as the hon. gentleman says this canal is in length, and keeping in a channel 110 feet wide ! It would be a pretty difficult thing to do in day time, especially when a vessel was passing out, but at night I do not see how it is possible even with a breadth of channel of 200 feet. I suppose the hon. gentleman has the whole channel lighted with electricity from the commencement to the end, so that ships would be able to use I he channel at night.

That does not come under my charge. There is already at Collingwood a large fleet of steamers. The Great Northern Navigation Company have a large fleet, and all their boats call at Collingwood. Collingwood is one of the most important points on the Georgian bay now.

Collingwood is a very prosperous town. A very large fleet of boats is now laid up there for the winter, and Collingwood is probably one of the largest grain shipping points on the lake. Nature never intended it for such a port, because, I suppose it is about as difficult and bad a harbour as we could find on the lakes; yet, the business has grown up there and shipping has made that a port to an extent not equalled by any other port on the lakes. I suppose, that being the case, the government must go on spending money, but it is going to cost a million dollars before they can make it a port such as it ought to be to accommodate the trade. Increased shipping must come there if the shipping continues to increase on the great lakes as it has done during the last three years. An enormous amount of money must be expended, because this is probably the most important shipping point on the great lakes.

The report of the engineer, after a very careful examination into the matter, is to the effect that with $120,000 of an expenditure we will be able to give a width to the whole channel of 200 feet.
. Mr. INGRAM. Last year there was $202,000 expended on the Collingwood harbour,
| there was $25,000 in the ordinary estimates

and |8,000 in tlie supplementary estimates besides $40,000 this year which would make a total of $275,000 expended on the Colling-wood harbour. Would the hon. gentleman tell us if these figures are correct, how much more he will require to complete Col-lingwood harbour and also what success the shipyard is meeting with there ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. I have just stated in discussing the position with my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) that the estimate of the engineer of the department, after a careful examination, is that with $120,000 we would be able to provide a channel 200 feet wide and 20 feet deep in Collingwood harbour. Besides this $40,000, if we want to go on with the widening of the channel, we will have to ask parliament to vote an additional sum of $80,000 to complete the channel to a width of 200 feet
Depot Hartcur-breakwater, $05,000.

There was an item last year for Depot harbour which the hon. minister will see, if he will look at page V-209, of the Auditor General's Report. I notice that for advertising, $029.61 was expended, and on King's Printer's account, $49.72. The money we are asked for here is for work to be done at Depot harbour. How was this money expended for advertising ?

Tenders were asked for the work, and the reason why the money was paid is that when tenders are asked for works of that importance, we, of course, advertise in more papers than we do when calling for tenders for smaller works. Tenders were asked and received, the lowest being that of Mr. J. T. Davis for $157,500. After the tenders were received, we discovered that soundings and borings had not been taken in a sufficient manner. Perhaps the committee will understand me better if I am able to show a plan of the harbour. If some of the hon. gentlemen who take an interest in this work will come to the Table, they may have a look at the plan. Here is the harbour and here is Mr. Booth's elevator. Here is an island. Mr. Booth has built all of that harbour with his own money. He is about the only man in the country who has built a harbour with his own cash, his own money and credit.
Where do you intend to spend the money ?
Here is the island. The entrance to the harbour is not sufficiently protected and it is intended to build this breakwater here.
What will it cost?
The lowest tender put in was for $157,500, but my engineers, taking for granted that

.
the examination and survey made by Mr. Booth's engineer were right, did not make the borings here, which they should have made. My hon. friend has been in the department and he knows what takes place often. When the tenders were received, I was warned by somebody that borings should be made. I went up myself with a boat, I had borings made and I find that instead of there being hard material in the bottom of the harbour such as we had supposed, there was silt carried in by the water We had provided for only four feet of settling in the crib-work, but instead of four feet, we discovered that the settling would be about fifteen feet. But, before discovering that, thinking that there would be only a few feet of settling, I had agreed with the contractor to give him so much per cubic yard to throw stone into the eribwork there, but I found out afterwards that it would settle fifteen feet and then I stopped the whole thing because the additional work necessary to make it safe would cost about $30,000. The whole matter is now before my colleagues.

Goderich harbour-dredging, $10,000.

There are two elevators, and a new one has been built during the last two years. Unfortunately that harbour is one of those on the lakes that fills. The piers were in a very bad condition, we had to repair them, and we had to dredge a good deal. If we were going to listen to all the demands made upon us, we would have built a large
