Was there not a plan adopted by your department some time ago, by which this silting of the sand would be prevented. There will be an eternal expenditure if you are goidg to dredge everv time after a storm.

I have received a petition which states that if there was a breakwater it would prevent the silting, but I doubt that very much. It would cost a large amount of money and I have not yet made up my mind to grant the petition.
I understand there was a plan recommended in regard to Port Dover and Goderich and a harbour in Prince Edward Island, in which the sand silts in a similar manner.
Toronto harbour is in the very same position. This silting of the sand is one of the most difficult problems we have to solve.
Are Martin & Co. doing the dredging there ? How are they getting on ?
Yes. They are getting on very well.
Were they the only contractors ?
Yes.
Did Mr. McGillicudy have anything to do with that work ?

Mr. McGillicudy had nothing to do with the dredging to my knowledge. He was the lowest tenderer on another contract and my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) might get work to-morrow if he does me the pleasure of tendering, and if he is the lowest tenderer.
If the minister's statement is correct, he cannot refer to the original contract.
That was a newspaper mistake. Mr. McGillicudy never got a contract for dredging although the papers said he did. He had a contract for the breakwater.
I never heard the report contradicted that he got a dredging contract.
It was contradicted in this House.
This work is done at the rate of $8 an hour. Have they taken out the number of yards required ?
The chief engineer explains that in certain parts of the work there was rock and hard pan, and of course they could not take out the 600 yards a day in that kind of work.
Is this the usual way of letting dredging contracts ?

I hope the time is not distant when the department will have enough dredges to do its own work. Dredging is now paid for at the rate of $8 an hour, 600 yards a day, making 13J cents a yard, and we have found no means of doing it cheaper unless we do it ourselves with modern dredges. That is the reason why I ask parliament for money to build dredges because they will do cheaper and quicker work.
Will the minister explain why he is paying 13J cents a yard here, when he is getting it done in Sarnia at 9} cents a yard ?
Tlie chief engineer explains that the work to which my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) objects-
The minister had better not put words in my mouth. I am simply asking for information and he has no right to say that I am objecting.
I am very glad my hon. friend does not object to the work. I was not here when that contract was given. There is dredging which costs less, but it all depends on the material which is dredged.
The minister has not yet explained why he paid 9J cents a yard in Sarnia and a larger sum at other places.
The chief engineer explains that that was a lump sum contract and it worked out in that way.
I hope the minister will lay on the Table after dinner the papers I asked for, namely, the contract, the tenders, the progress estimates, and so on.
That cannot be done to-day.
Then you had better let the item stand.

I am asking $75,000 for general dredging and we will discuss it on that vote. I pledge myself to bring down the papers. It is nearly six o'clock now and the employees have left their offices. I cannot get the papers to-night. I will bring them down with pleasure on Monday.

This item does not come under the vote for general dredging. There was a specific sum voted for it last year, and it has appeared in the estimates many years. The hon. gentleman had not the courage of his convictions, to spend the money until after the elections ; but as he repented and spent it some time, I am not disposed to raise objections to the work. I simply inquired whether it was to be continued.
I did not understand what my hon. friend wanted. I pledge myself to bring down the papers on Monday, and lay them on the Table of the House.

I notice that the principle of paying $8 an hour for dredging is in vogue in different parts of the country. I would like to ask the minister if the dredges which are paid at that rate are of the same capacity, and is there an officer of the government on the dredges to check the time ?

All the dredges are not of the same capacity, but we exact from them 600 yards a day. There is an officer on board each dredge, and at the end of the month we make up the figures, and we only pay according to that rate.

It seems to me the work would be done much more cheaply if the contract were at so much a yard. I can understand that a dredge working by the hour, even if there were a government officer around, would do less work than if working by the yard. What is the objection to doing it by the yard ?

Because we have tried it, and it has always cost more. I hope the House will agree with me that it is time for us to do our own dredging at a cheap rate. With a modern dredge you can always be sure to do the work for three or four cents a yard. We are now paying thirteen cents a yard. I am proud to say that we are doing it at much less than other departments, although I do not find any fault with them.
Does the hon. gentleman ever expect to have dredges enough at his disposal to go from one end of Canada to the other and do these small parcels of work ?

Yes, I expect, within two years, at the beginning of the season following the coming season, to be able to carry on our work in Ontario, or most of it. We are building at Sorel one large dredge, and we are beginning to build another one. We have in British Columbia a small suction dredge, which dredges about 12,000 yards a day, and I am building one for Ontario on the same lines. There is a vast difference between that and the small dredges which do only GOO yards a day.
Will the hon. minister inform me how many dredges the government claims to own ?
My officers tell me that we own nineteen.
How many more does he -think the government will require in order to meet the calls on his department for dredging ?

The number would be sufficient, in my opinion, if all the dredges were up to date. For instance, the large dredge which we are building at Sorel for the maritime provinces will alone do more work than all the dredges we have in those provinces at present.

The hon. gentleman has frequently told me that he has been unable for the want of dredges to complete some work I have applied for time and again in my county. Will the hon. minister Mr. KEMP.
come under a contract with me to employ dredges which I will build, and pay me the same amount of money that he is now paying to other parties for doing that service ?
If the hon. member were unwise enough to enter into such a contract, he would lose his seat, and I would not like to see him leave the House.
I would run that risk.
The hon. gentleman might adopt the plan followed by a member of parliament who owns a dredge on the Georgian bay, but keeps it in the name of some friends.
I do not do anything of the kind.
The hon. gentleman misunderstands me. I did not say he did it. He knows the case I refer to, because it is notorious.

It is a bad case if it is true.
Kingsville-repairs to wharf and breakwater piers and extension of western piers, $15,000.
Explain this ?

It is composed of a revote of $5,000 and a new vote of $10,000 to complete the work. Kingsville is in Essex county. Governments past and present have spent a pretty large sum of money on this harbour. The total expenditure up to the 31st December last was $85,951. I spent up to the 31st December, $7,836, and I expect to spend up to the 30th June, $7,000 additional, to complete the work, that is, to extend one pier, to make repairs to the piers, and to dredge a little.
Will the hon. gentleman give us an idea of the number of boats that run in and out there ?

I have in my hand a note to this effect, that this harbour is much resorted to for shelter by vessels of small tonnage and light draught. There is a regular line of steamers running between Windsor and Pelee Island, which calls at that place.
Meaford Harbour, Out.-dredging and pile works, $30,000.
In what condition is the dredging ?

The contractor, Mr. Piggott, is going on fairly well now-better than in the past- and we expect the work to be completed shortly. There is not only dredging but an extension of the pier and some sheet piling work. The work will be completed, I hope, in the month of September.
About how much dredging remains to be done ?
About half the dredging has been done.
Has there been any application made for piling on the west side of the harbour ?
1 do not remember, but no doubt some applications will be made. I remember now that there has been a verbal application.
How far was the breakwater extended out ?
Three hundred feet.
Is the dredging along the wharf and the elevator finished.

The dredging has been carried out the whole way in deep water. Meaford is one of the harbours in which I have great confidence indeed. There is a large trade there, and the Grand Trunk Railway is encouraging them to build a large elevator.

I am glad to know that the hon. minister hopes to finish this work at an early date. Some more important work will still be needed on the west side, but the work so far as it has gone, has given great satisfaction. The dredging done so far enables the largest vessels to reach the elevator. -And although the dredging was only completed late in the fall, over a million and a half bushels of grain were handled in that elevator last fall. And as the road from there to Collingwood is very level, it is one of the points where the Grand Trunk railway can handle grain very easily. There is deep enough water close to the end of the dock to float the largest vessels that sail on the lake. What is most urgently needed now is dredging, and the people are grateful for what the hon. minister has done so far.
Midland Harbour-dredging, $8,000.
How much was expended last year and what was paid for the dredging per hour ?
I have not got that information under my hand, but will bring it down Monday.
In what part of the bay . was the money expended ?

We have deepened the channel just at the entrance, as my hon. friend knows, leading to the large smelting milL I have spent the money where the Grand Trunk Railway and the smelting people asked me to spend it, and tried to guide my action by the requirements of the large interests concerned in Midland. Midland, like Collingwood, is one of the most thriving ports on the Georgian Bay, and if the Grand Trunk Railway do what I understand some of their people intend doing, we may have pretty large results there. If the Grand Trunk Railway make up their minds to double their track from Midland to the city of Montreal, we will have a large amount of traffic at that port.

I have no objection to the expenditure on dredging last year, but the dredging has not been done in what is known as the harbour proper. The harbour is one and a half mile wide, and some years ago docks were built there by the Grand Trunk Railway, but the receding waters necessitated dredging in front of these docks. I think that considerable of the money has been expended in that way.
We have from time to time vessels carrying a quarter of a million bushels of grain and even of greater capacity, so that a very considerable depth of water is required. As to the money expended at the smelter, that expenditure is a commendable one. That concern is one of very considerable proportions, with a pay roll of $13,000 a month. These docks were not built in sufficiently deep water, and the money was spent last year in dredging opposite the smelter, so as to give two or three feet more water and accommodate larger vessels.
The Grand Trunk is asking us to give a depth of 20 feet.
That is necessary.

Up to the 30th November last we spent during the last two years $15,000 in dredging. I am just now giving more attention to this port in view of the statements made to me by the railway companies, and I cannot say what will be the result of the information that is conveyed to me. I cannot say what we may do in the supplementary estimates, but I must state once more my firm hope that we will not lose sight of the necessity of doing everything to improve our St. Lawrence route. If the railway companies want to work with us from a Canadian standpoint. I have no doubt that the government and the House of Commons will understand the position and do the right thing at the right time.

I think that the proposed expenditure during the coming season will commend itself to the citizens of the town. These two large elevators had originally twenty feet of water. But within the last ten years, the waters of the Georgian Bay have receded three or four feet. I think it is quite right to restore the depth of twenty feet, as proposed.
Is it possible that Midland requires $8,000 for dredging ? I always understood that there was plenty of water there.
To do the dredging that ought to be done there would require about $50,000.

Perhaps it would be as well for the minister to tell us where Midland Is. I have heard a great deal about it but never saw it. It is proposed to expend $8,000, but the minister says it will require $50,000. If this harbour is necessary and the expenditure Is necessary to the harbour, by all means do the work well while you are at it.
Where is Midland ?

That is what I want to know. I will get there if I live.
Oakville-repairs to east pier, &c., $4,000.

This is to complete the work.
Owen Sound Harbour-dredging and pile protection to works, $24,000.

This is under contract.
Port Hope'-repairs to piers, $5,000.

This is to complete the work.
I'resqu'Isle-purchase of wharf and repairs, $2,500.
I move that that item be struck out.
There was a grant last year of $5,000 for Presqu'Isle harbour. Was any of that spent 7
No. And I am moving to strike out this item.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why was the item put in 7
Because I thought it could be used. I went to negotiate for the purchase, but the price was too high, so I made up my mind not to do it at all.

Motion agreed to.
River Ottawa-improvement of narrows at Petewawa, above Pembroke, $4,000.
This is an old contract which was in existence when we took office. It is a work of dredging in the Ottawa, by Mr. Poupore.
Mr. Poupore is the contractor ?
Yes, Mr. George Poupore.
How much has been expended, and for what object ?
We have paid no money. It is a bulk contract for $7,000. It is not completed, and we have not paid a cent. The work is going on now. I saw it when I was up there last year.
What navigation can there be on the Petawawa ?
There is certainly navigation there. I passed there in a steamer last season.
We should concentrate our efforts upon the Ottawa river and the Georgian Bay canal and not upon these smaller streams.

My hon. friend is mistaken. This is for the removal of shoal in the Ottawa river. The contract was given in 1895. But, on account of a mistake which Mr. Poupore said he made, he found that, instead of sand, he had to take out stone and hard-pan. So you can see he is not going very fast.
This, then, is for the improvement of the navigation of the Ottawa opposite the entrance of the Petawawa ?
Yes.
If I may be permitted, I would like to ask a question concerning the item about Presqu'Isle. Would the hon. minister tell us why no money has been spent and the item is now dropped 7
So far, not a cent has been spent, I believe.

Last year, when the hon. minister asked for this sum of money he said that hundreds of Liberals and Conservatives had sought to have this work done. He said this was a very fine country and the work was really necessary. Why did he drop it 7

I tried to purchase the work but they asked too much. Is the hon. gentleman displeased that I did not buy it 7 He was displeased last year when I proposed to buy it, and now I understand he is displeased that I have decided not to buy it. I do not know exactly what I am to do to satisfy the hon. gentleman.

Instead of being displeased I am very much pleased, and I commend the course the hon. minister has taken. This is in accordance with what I told him, that when he is right I am ready to stand up and declare my approval, just as I am ready to condemn him when he deserves it. I do not seek to make party capital out of this matter-there are plenty of chances beside; this.

I wish to call the attention of the hon. minister to a promise he made last summer in the riding of East

Simcoe. I would like to read an item from a newspaper, and after he has heard It read, I hope he will devote the money he at first intended for Presqu'Isle to this dock which he promised at Orillia. The Orillia ' News Letter ' says :
You will remember the beautiful summer evening last July when the Hon. J. Israel Tarte stopped oft here for an hour or so, and incidentally took a jaunt down to Couchiching Beach along with the mayor and some of the councillors. The band was at the park on this particular evening, as were also about 1,500 townspeople composed mostly of Orillia's gayly dressed fair sex. It was just the usual Friday night at the park, but to the minister the scene was a revelation. In fact, so enchanting was it he immediately promised us, as he stood on the shore and waved his hand along the beach, a new $3,000 wharf right away. 'I make this bequest on account of the many beautiful ladies,' said the Honourable Israel. This was very gallant, indeed, and the ladies all appreciated it, as did also the rest of the townspeople as we thought the long-felt want would he at last fulfilled. We failed to write it on a card and attach the same to his person so he has forgotten. And to think he would go back on the ladies ! Barrie is to get $3,000 for its new wharf. Oh! Israel.
In view of the solemn and gallant promise made to the ladies, I hope the hon. minister will put in the supplementary estimates the money he intended for Presqu'Isle, and devote it to the wharf at Orillia.
On a beautiful evening in the month of August last I had the pleasure of calling at Orillia. It is a fine town, with a beautiful park, and I must confess
You were seduced.

I was seduced by the beauty of the ladies of that town, by their elegance, and by the great kindness They showed to a poor little French Canadian Minister who was travelling into those parts of the country. Well, I did not make a formal promise, but I went pretty far. I spoke of $3,000-yes, I think I mentioned the figure. I said if a vote of $3,000 will build a wharf, I will ask my colleagues to allow me to do so. There were splendid yachts on the lake. Really, it Is one of the most beautiful lakes, one of the most beautiful places, in the country. I expect to fulfil my promise. I try not to go back on the ladies. I have never been accused of that so far.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Bill ( No. 36) to incorporate the British Columbia and Yukon Railway Company.- Mr. Riley.
Bill (No. 37) to incorporate the Sprague's Falls Manufacturing Company, Limited.- Mr. Emmerson.

House again in Committee of Supply.
River St. Lawrence-dredging steamboat channel through shoal at foot of Wolf Island, $10,000.

The object of this work is to dredge a channel at the foot of Wolf Island to allow steamers to call at Kingston, and then go over to the American waters. X have made a complete survey of the whole work. It is to allow American boats to take supplies at Canadian ports.
Does this cover the whole of the dredging ?

At the foot of the island, yes.
Sault. St3. Ma;L-harbour improvements, including dredging of approaches, $25,000.

Every one knows that we have not enough water to allow Canadian boats to go to our wharfs. Canadian boats passing through the Canadian, Sault Ste. Marie canal, are obliged to go to the American side to load and unload. I am going to give an additional depth of water so as. to allow them to go to the wharfs on the Canadian side.
What is the amount which will be required to finish the work 1
Has this been let by contract, and if so, who has the contract ?
We have not given any contract as yet.
You have not expended any money as yet ?
No.
Well then, I want a promise from the hon. minister that he will let it by contract unless he has a dredge of his own.

Very well, I have no objection to do that.

I am perfectly ready to ask for tenders. If my hon. friend will allow me, perhaps, I will make a promise that is not in the right direction. I have had a long experience in the House. I will ask for tenders and make a test. It is quite possible that the man who will be the lowest tenderer will not have the plant necessary to perform the work. I will make a test of it. It has happened before, often and often since I have been in office, that a man who has put in the lowest tender has not the equipment necessary to do the work.

We must insist that the Order in Council shall be carried out which provides that where there is an expenditure over a certain amount, tenders shall be asked for and the contract given to the lowest tenderer. If the hon. minister has a dredge of his own which he can use for the purpose it is all right, but if not, we must insist upon tenders being asked for.
I have a perfect right to do otherwise, but I will ask for tenders in this case just to make a test of it. Let us not discuss the Order in Council now; I will make a test of it.

Suppose it costs a higher amount, it is better in the public interest and it is better in the interests of public morality that a contract should be given although it costs a higher amount unless the department has a dredge available for the purpose.
I will do it this time.

There seem to be conflicting rumors as to the depth of water in the Sault Ste. Marie canal. I would like to ask the hon. minister what is the depth of water in the Soo canal on the mitre sill, and how much money would be required to complete the dredging sufficient to give a uniform depth of water. It was put at 19 or 20 feet before.

I cannot speak as to the depth of water in the canal myself. That is not in my charge, and I do not like to speak of a matter in another department. I speak only of the dredging in the harbour itself. When my hon. colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) is in his seat, if the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) renews his question, I am sure he will get the information he desires.

The hon. Minister of Public Works is asking for authority to spend money in the harbour, and the approaches to the Soo canal so as tdP improve them for the purposes of navigation. He should have some plans before him showing the depth of water there, and how much dredging is required to give the uni-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
form depth of water that he requires for navigation.

I have a plan and a survey of the work I am going to carry out, but I must ask the hon. gentleman not to say that I should give information in regard to a matter that does not belong to me. My hon. friend is asking me to give him the depth of water on the mitre sill of the canal. The canal is not under my control; it is under the control of my colleague the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. As to the harbour it is of an unequal depth. There are spots where there are 15 feet of water and there are other places where there are IS feet. We are going to give a uniform depth of 20 feet.
At the approaches as well as in the canal?
The canal I do not want to speak of. My colleague the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals knows more about it than I do.

The depth of water on the mitre sill of the lock of the Sault Ste. Marie canal is the same as that of the canal on the American side, namely, 20 feet. In order to have a 20 foot navigation you want to dredge the approaches to the wharfs and to the locks and to provide more than 20 feet of water. You require to provide for a 21 foot navigation.
In the canal, I take it, there is 20 feet of water, and the hon. Minister of Public Works will endeavour to have a uniform depth of 20 feet in the harbour.
Yes.
You want to go one foot deeper.
The chief engineer reminds me that when I say 20 feet, I mean 20 feet clear. If I am not mistaken we have only 19$ feet on the mitre sill of the Canadian canal.
Are there only 19$ feet on the mitre sill ?
That is only my information; it is not in my department.

We want to settle this question. The member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says the depth is 20 feet, but I have heard it emphatically denied that it is 20 feet. We ought to have a statement from somebody who is able to state authoritatively what the depth Is.

My colleague, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, has in his estimates an item for dredging the approaches to the canal,

and when that Item ds tinder consideration the hon. member for East Grey can get an answer to that question. X do not want him to insist upon me giving an answer in regard to a matter which belongs to another department.
Where is this, dredging to be done ?
It is in the harbour; it is not in the canal at all.

The item is only here for one year, and that is not so long. We are preparing the contract now. Southampton is an important port especially in view of the fact that Mr. Clergue is going to build the Algoma Central Railway, and Southampton is expected to be one of its terminals. The contract is under way. It is an extension of the landing pier so as to stop the filling up of the harbour. When that extension is made, a little dredging will make it a very good harbour indeed.
It says 'dredging of approaches.'
It does not mean the approaches to the canal. The harbours are under my care and the canals and their approaches are under the control of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals.
Except from Nipissing to the Georgian Bay.

That is not a canal. The improvement of rivers is not under the care of the Department of Railways and Canals although they have done a good deal in the past which they had no right to do. The lakes are not under the charge of the Railway Department. There is no doubt as to that.
I have secured legal opinion upon that point, but in this case the question does not arise because it is purely and simply a harbour work.

I misunderstood that.
I thought it meant the approaches to the canal.
The control of the rivers, or the deepening of them, depends entirely on whether the hon. minister is able to impress his individuality on the rest of the government or not.

I do not think it depends on that at all, because the law is perfectly clear. The rivers and lakes are under the Public Works Department, but I may say that in the past the individuality of the Minister of Railways and Canals impressed itself a little too much. I certainly would not allow that now for this excellent reason that the Railways and Canals constitute one department and the Public Works another department. I feel quite able to carry out the work that is under my care, as my colleague, I have no doubt, feels quite able to carry out the work under his care.
Southampton-improvement of harbour, $10,000.
What is going to be done here ? For how many years will we find this item appearing in the estimates before it is used ?
What dredging has been done this year ?
We have not dredged this year in that part of the harbour. We have dredged in the river.
What kind of an improvement is this ?
It is an extension of the pier so as to form a kind of closed harbour with an entrance. We will dredge inside the harbour when that extension is completed, and it will not fill up again.
How much will this work cost when finished ?
The whole thing, extension and dredging, will cost in the neighbourhood of $50,000.
And you are commencing an undertaking here which means $50,000 ?
Which may mean $50,000.
But the minister must have some definite data to justify him in asking this vote.
When completed the work will cost in the neighbourhood of $50,000.
It will be let by contract ?
Yes.

Before this vote is adopted, I would like to ask the minister a question oi' two. This is the harbour to which Mr. Clergue is building his railroad, but there is before the government a petition asking that certain improvements should be made in Tobermory harbour. Tobermory is one of the most important harbours on the lake, and I think myself that it is probably the best harbour on Lake; Huron. At times you will find fifteen or twenty vessels in that harbour. They have no dock to tie up to and the government has never expended any money there. It would be of very great public utility if improvements were made at Tobermory harbour to facilitate the shipping on the lake.

I trust that when the supplementary estimates come down the minister will see lit to include an appropriation for the building of a dock at Tobermory harbour.

We have received a request for harbour works at that place. The chief engineer tells me that we have given instructions that a complete survey shall be made. When that survey has been completed I will be in a position to say more than I can now in reference to Tobermory harbour.

In addition to what my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Halli-day) has said, I would point out that Tobermory, or 'the Tub,' as it is familiarly called, is one of the most wonderful harbours to be found on the continent. It would seem as though nature herself had planted it there as a refuge for sailors in stress of weather. I have never understood that there was particular necessity for docks there, but there is certainly a great necessity for having proper iron hooks and things of that kind placed in the rocks so that boats may be tied up. I would not say that docks are not necessary, and my hon. friend (Mr. Halliday) can speak with very great authority on that point. Those who are conversant with the shipping on the lakes know that Tobermory harbour is a perfect Godsend to mariners, and the department could not do better than direct its attention to improving that place.

The next time I go up there I will see that harbour.
St. Joseph, Lake Huron-wharf, $5,000.
Might I ask the Minister of Public Works what will be the total cost of that wharf when it is completed ?

Even if no question had been asked, I would have given some explanation as to that work. St. Joseph is on Lake Huron, between Goderich and Bayfield. Two years ago, two deputations came to see me, one from Montreal and one from the county of Huron. It was represented to me that French Cana, dians had been induced to come from Chicago and settle there in large numbers. Mr. Cantin and the priest headed that deputation. They represented to me that they had organized a plan of immigration, that there was a saw-mill to be established, and that there was a brick yard with a large trade.
Is the saw-mill there at present ?

Yes, there is a small saw-mill and a brick yard there also, though not a very large one.
I will place myself in the hands of the House and state the case fully. That argument was advanced to me by the people who had Mr. HALLIDAY.
already settled there. A gentleman by the name of Cantin was at the head of the whole thing. Mr. Macmillan, the then member for the riding, was favourable to the project. 1 had a preliminary survey made. Then a deputation came from Montreal. Mr. Val-lee, who I am sorry is dead now, was at the head of that deputation. I knew him very well. He was a large hotel owner, and an enterprising man, and a man of substance. He represented to me that he had formed a company to build a large summer resort hotel. This was two years ago, and the hotel has been undertaken but not completed. I placed an amount in the estimates on these representations that I submitted to my colleagues. On the representations that were made in Chicago and which were, I suppose, the same as made to me, a certain number of families, I believe about twenty-five families, came from Chicago and settled there. The brick yard was started; the hotel was started, and so on. I may say that the village has not made a great deal of progress. I think there are about 150 people who have left Chicago to settle there, and the priest who lives there came to see me again three or four weeks ago. I did not know whether to ask my colleagues and the House to leave this item in the estimates or not. This gentleman with two or three others came to me and represented to me that if we did not discourage them, there would be a considerable immigration from Chicago and other American centres to that place. On the strength of these statements I have allowed the item to remain in the estimates. There is the whole thing in two words.
The hon. gentleman has not answered my question, what is this harbour going to cost when finished ?

I am not going to spend more than $8,000 there. There was $5,000 given already, and I ask for $3,000 more. My engineers have given special attention to that harbour, especially Mr. Roy, whom I sent there, and they state that $8,000 will be sufficient for the requirements of the work. They say that a small brick yard which is there at present will develop, and will do an export trade in brick to Chicago. Those people are settled there rightly or wrongly. I state the case as it has been represented to me, and I leave it in the hands of the House.
What depth of water will this wharf give 1
Between eight and ten feet.
Have you purchased the land 1
No, I have not. I have not done anything yet, except survey the place carefully.
Wlio owns the land ?

I do not know. In point of fact, I have done nothing. There has been a stoppage of the whole thing. I think it is an interesting place. I believe there will be a large immigration there. We are paying large sums of money to bring people from Russia, Poland, and all parts of the world, and I thought it would be a good thing to bring a few dozen French Canadians to invade Ontario.
How much will this work cost when completed ? What is the enterprise that will bring them there ?
I have just stated that there is a saw mill and a small brick yard.

It seems to me that this is a very extraordinary state of affairs. While I have the honour to represent North Middlesex, I live in the county of Huron.
I have lived from a boy in the township in which this work is going on, and know this place very well, and I can assure the House that this hotel, which the hon. gentleman says was not finished four years ago, is not finished to-day.
I admit that.

I cannot come to any other conclusion than that the hon. minister has been misled. I am not aware that there is any such immigration there as he speaks of. I live within a few miles of the place, and have been through it, and I would not like to say that there are twenty-five families there altogether. It is true, it has a post office and a saw-mill, and a dock would be necessary to enable the mill to get logs, because there is no timber in that part of the country to supply a saw-mill. It is an old and settled part of the country. There are a few French families there who came from Lower Canada.
From Chicago.

I beg pardon. You can hardly find a family there that came from Chicago. There are French Canadians who came from Lower Canada forty or fifty years ago and settled in that part of the country. The gentleman whom the hon. minister has referred to came there a few years ago and started a hotel and built the saw-mill. There are a few respectable dwellings there, but most are not completed. I believe Mr. Cantin owns them. I can assure the hon. minister that the people of that section of the country do not look on an expenditure at this place as being a proper expenditure of public money. I have here a paper from which I might read a short 40
extract. This paper is edited by a leading Reformer, who holds the position of county councillor, and who has always taken an active part in the affairs of the Liberal party. This is the ' Brussels Post.'
Is Brussels far from that place ?
It is in the county of Huron. I do not know exactly how far it is.
About thirty miles.

Perhaps it is. This paper says :
Wo notice that a delegation ot big and little politicians recently visited St. Joseph, on the shores of Lake Huron, with the intent of the expenditure of money for harbour or dock purposes. St. Joseph's needs a harbour as badly as a goose requires side pockets, and any such expenditure is just that much money thrown away as fr.r as serving the public. A harbour ' is not required there, nor is there any probability of it ever being used if it were there. Surely there has been .money enough squandered by both political parties in the past in breakwaters, docks, harbours, &c., without continuing this nonsensical work any longer. No person can object to legitimate expenditure in necessary public works, hut why members do not protest against the misuse of moneys that should be applied to other purposes, we fail to make out. Tf 'wilful waste makes woeful want' then it is about time that somebody called a halt, and the 'Post' for one says somebody should be brought sharply to time if this kind of work is continued. We could mention so-called harbours on which thousands of dollars were spent and they are in worse shape to-day than 10 years ago, and do not nor never did even begin to pay a tithe of the interest on the money foolishly spent, nor serve any practical purpose.
Now, this is what a friend of the government has said. I am sorry that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) is not in his place tonight ; for he had the honour at one time ns he stated this afternoon, of representing the riding in which this place is situated, and he knows the extent of the public sentiment which the minister speaks of. He knows that it was from the province of Quebec that these gentlemen came. One thing I am pleased with is that the Chairman of this Committee (Mr. Macdonald, East Huron) is a member for the county where this work is going on. I am satisfied that the hon. members of this House are too conscientious to advocate expenditure of this kind, and I think the government should have some fixed principle on which to proceed in their expenditure of the public money, instead of doing, as they are in this item, voting an expenditure of $7,000 or $8,000, to favour some political friends.

I do not see what there is in the plea that in this case we are giving money to friends. Why, there is scarcely an elector in the



*place, so that there cannot be any political *object in this vote. I have stated the facts, [DOT]as I think very frankly. It was represented to me, when the item was placed in the [DOT]estimates, that this was a good beginning of a settlement. And $5,000 is not a large amount of money. It makes one smile rather to see people like my hon. friend making a big mountain out of this expenditure of $5,000, when much larger expenditures in Ontario and the other provinces are voted by them without a word or the slightest hint of scandal. That is not the kind of conduct that is likely to impress me very much. The question is whether, in this case we should go on with the expenditure or not. The government were right, and the House was right in placing this item in the estimates, but I must admit that our expectations have not yet materialized. And what I ask the House now is to vote the item, and I pledge myself to visit the place personally, and if I am not satisfied that there is justification for this expenditure, I will not make it. I pledge myself that if there is no public good to be served by this expenditure, it will not be made. In the meantime, I shall not spend a dollar before examining into the thing myself. I do not suppose that I can be asked to do more than that.
Hon. Mr. IIAGGAItT. This is a new idea of responsibility. The hon. minister asks the House to vote the amount and then tells us that if, after personal visit and examination, he finds it is not required, he pledges his honour not to spend it. But he should know the whole circumstances before asking for the money. That is the principle of ministerial responsibility. He has no right to ask us to vote the item after the statement he has just made. He should be frank enough now to tell the House that as he is not fully informed of the circumstances he will withdraw the item. For what purpose does he ask the vote ? For the purpose of inducing settlement from Chicago into a section of country which has been settled in every part of it, for forty years. That was the reason given by him, and now that he admits it he was Dot fully informed, he ought to withdraw the item.

I cannot do that, for the excellent reason that I have taken every possible precaution against any unnecessary expenditure being made. I am fully prepared to take my share of the responsibility. I pledge myself to the House to go there personally and investigate the whole matter. My hon. friend says that I should know all the circumstances now. Well, I sent a special engineer up there, Mr. Roy, and he gave me the report I have stated. Of course I am now in a rather difficult position from a certain standpoint. Here is a French Canadian settlement, and I am a
French Canadian minister, and I will be accused in the press of asking the House to vote a special sum in favour of a French settlement.
Oh, oh.
Nobody else but the hon. minister has mentioned anything of the kind.
It is just as well to go straight to the point in a case like this. I have nothing to gain in this business. Do I understand hon. gentlemen opposite to say that I should withdraw the vote ?

Yes, from the
statement the hon. minister has made.
What statement ?

His statement
that he pledged himself to the House to make inquiries afterwards.
Personal inquiries.

That he would make inquiries afterwards, and if he found the circumstances did not warrant the expenditure he would not make it. When a minister asks the House to vote an expenditure, he thereby assures the House that he has made thorough inquiries; but from the statement of the Minister of Public Works, he has not the necessary information to justify his asking the House to vote this money.

Half of the votes placed in the estimates are placed there before there is even a survey made. In this case there has been a survey made and full examination, but in view of the fact that Mr. Cantin does not seem to have realized all the expectations he held out with regard to certain people, I shall not spend the money before making a personal visit myself. I have some other business to bring me there, and I shall be there in a month or so after the House adjourns, and I say that I will not spend a dollar of the money unless I find that there is a good scheme of immigration under way. If there is a scheme to have families come in from the United States or elsewhere to settle there on a pretty large scale, I shall ask my colleagues to allow me to spend the money, but if there is not I shall not. I think that that is a fair statement.

It is not a constitutional manner of treating the question at all. Besides who was it raised the question of prejudice or of opposition to the vote on account of twenty-five French families being there ? Why is it that in a little matter of this kind, the Minister of

Public Works should descend to racial prejudice ?
I did not do it.

The hon. gentleman is the only person who mentioned at all the fact of twenty-five French families being there, and he ascribed our opposition to the vote to that fact, and to his intention to induce other French families to emigrate into that section. Why does he make an appeal of that kind on a little question of voting a few thousand dollars for a harbour, which he can justify on no other ground ? It is the smallest kind of political manoeuvring that I ever witnessed in the House, and the Minister of Public Works will have to rise above that kind of tactics. He may appeal to racial prejudices on other questions, but it is perfectly absurd to appeal to them on a vote for a little harbour that no one in that section has heard of or requires. It is the smallest kind of parish politics that I ever heard introduced into this House.
Parish politics is not the kind of politics that I resort to. I do not see that my hon. friend is in any way justified in talking as he has done. I have not a word to take back of what I said.
Make an apology, and do not do it again.

I have not a word to take back. I say that I shall not spend the money until I make myself personally acquainted with all the facts and circumstances, and we will see now whether or not I shall not be accused-I do not say that I will be accused here-I know that my hon. friend is above that kind of thing; I know him too well to believe for one moment that anything of the kind will come to his mind. Permit me to say that I have not the slightest intention of ascribing anything of the kind to him. I have been accused in the press about different affairs. This time, I must plead 1 not guilty,' because there is no ground to commit anything of the kind.
Don't do it again.

The minister says that the fact of the item being in the estimates has induced some people to settle there, and that this is a reason for putting the item in the estimates this year. What then, induced the hon. gentleman to put it in in the first place ?

I have already stated that two deputations came to me, one of them from Montreal, composed of people I know very well. Unfortunately one of these gentlemen is dead. Mr. Vallee, who was a well known man among the members of parliament, and a man of means. They told me that they wished to establish a summer resort and build a hotel. The proof that such a scheme was a genuine one, is that the hotel ha* been started-a large structure. Unfortunately, as I have said, Mr. Vallee died. Among the gentlemen who accompanied him when he came to see me were a number of men of substance from Montreal, men I knew very well. Afterwards Mr. Cantin, the parish priest and half a dozen other people represented that they had organized an immigration scheme and that Chicago families were going to come in. These deputations induced us to place the item in the estimates. I simply ask to be allowed to investigate the case before doing anything more. If there is not an expectation of any large settlement there I will not spend the money.

The hon. minister gives as his reason why this item should pass that there was no objection to it last year. On that basis of reasoning, why did he move to strike out an item-as he did just before six o'clock-which had passed last year ?
I have already explained the case of Presqu'Isle.
Not satisfactorily to this opposition.
If my hon. friend is not pleased, perhaps I could put the item back again in the estimates.
The hon. minister said that it is the duty of the opposition to criticise these items.
I do not complain.

Now we -feel that the hon. minister has not given us sufficient information to justify us in supporting this item. One of the reasons against it is that a paper published in the riding in which the money was to be expended has denounced it, and the editor of that paper is a supporter of this government. We also find that an hon. gentleman who represents part of the territory contained within Huron county, de-

nounced this item. And the minister himself gives us no good reason for supporting it, but tells us to pass the item and he will investigate the item. It would be better to investigate first and be ready to give information to the committee to justify them in passing the item. The hon. minister also sneered at the House on account of the French families living there. I wish to point out to him the delicate position we would be in if we accepted his advice. He says that there are twenty-five French families there. He has been accused as he says himself in the public press of favouring the French element in this country. If he goes to investigate the case, is it not the fact that they will expect more from him than they would from an English speaking minister, and might unduly influence him to expend this money, or perhaps, even a| larger sum. If he does not want to be put in this position, all he has to do is to allow the item to stand, or withdraw it. He can then investigate. And, if the expenditure is justified, he can come and ask it from the House next session.

This is an extraordinary proposition that the hon. minister makes to us. I confess that I admire his sterling enterprise when he wishes to do a good thing. But I am afraid he sometimes shows the same zeal when he wishes to do a bad thing. And I am afraid he has stumbled upon something like that to-night. In the first place, the principle of asking the House to vote money without giving reasons for it, is wrong. To vote money first and investigate afterwards is hardly the way parliament should do business. The plea is raised that a certain enterprising gentleman, who, I believe, has a paper town to sell there, is bringing in immigration. For what purpose ? We are told that a mill is to be put up there. But, on the other hand, we hear that there is no timber to supply a mill. They are going to establish a brick yard, we are told, and there will be no possibility of vessels coming in to carry the brick to Chicago. But to start brickmaking in Canada, with a view to sending the product several hundreds of miles to Chicago and putting them on the market there against a heavy duty, and, in importing immigrants for that purpose- is that the object aimed at in building this breakwater ? The hon. gentleman can spend this amount of money much better in some other way. This is an old settled country- it has been settled for fifty years anyway. There is nothing there to start an enterprise. It is said it will become a summer resort. Why, there is not a decent grove there for a summer resort. You have to start it on a bare shore. It is said there is a hotel there. A hotel has been in the course of construction for several years, but it is not finished, because there has been no inducement to finish it; as lawyers some-

times say of their cases, it is in statu quo. The minister says : Vote this money, and I will go on and make inquiry. He thinks that is sufficient excuse for voting the money. I want to ask the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McEwen), who lives in that county, whether he advises the expenditure of this money ?
This is a proposition to throw so much money away, or else to help some person. The minister does not even know who owns the land upon which it is proposed to build this dock. So far as we are told, it is the same man who has tried to build up a summer resort, it is the same man who is trying to sell his lot, the same man who is trying to make the public believe that the place can be built up by means of a brickyard. The idea of starting a brickyard there to make bricks for export to Chicago seems to be the wildest scheme I ever heard proposed to this House. There is nothing to support a saw-mill. There are no manufacturing establishments, nothing to begin a village. There are a few families there, and that is all the information we have. I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, who knows the locality well, will you get up and defend it ? I would ask the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McEwen) if he will get up and defend It. Let this House know if they think it is desirable that that money should be spent.

There has not been one dollar spent yet.
am surprised that the members of the opposition become excited at this paltry sum of money. In the days of Sir John A. Macdonald I remember that we did not get excited at a little thing like that, we were looking for bigger things. Here is my position. I have not spent a dollar of that money, and my hon. friend talks as if I had pledged the country to an expenditure of a million dollars. I pledge myself not to spend one dollar before I look carefully and personally into that case. But on the faith of that vote, for which my hon. friends are just as responsible as I am, the people have settled there. Is it not a reasonable proposition ? I think that the standpoint taken by the hon. gentlemen opposite is altogether wrong. I have not spent one dollar, and do not propose to, unless I am convinced that it is useful, and unless my colleagues to whom I must appeal are convinced that it will be a wise expenditure of money. For it is a question of confidence, after all, whether this House will trust me with' that small amount of money. If I am not going to be trusted for that amount of money, I might just as well pass to the other side.

The hon. minister seems to look upon it as a very small amount, but I do not think that this country can afford to let a minister run round through the country with these small amounts. I do not

think it is fair that we should be asked to authorize him to do a work of that kind. But the matter may not be as small as it appears. I am not an expert in harbour building, but 1 may mention that it is a shallow beach, a person can easily wade out into it ten or twelve rods. The minister this afternoon told us about a sum of $70,000 spent in Bayfield for a harbour. But this is a much harder place in which to build a harbour than was Bayfield. I think that $5,000 or even $8,000 will not accomplish the end that he mentions here. Indeed I do not think there is anything at this place to warrant such an undertaking. I am of the same opinion as that gentleman who is in the [DOT]county council, a leading Reformer, who stated in his paper that there was no use for the work. It is about ten miles from Bayfield, perhaps a little more. I have no idea that that dock will ever be used if it is built. It seems to me the minister is very easily convinced when he wants to construct a public work in any place. Even though it is a paltry amount of $5,000 or $8,000, he seems to be easily convinced that it is a proper expenditure, although the only argument he can make for it is that the town is a good place for a brickyard. We all know what a brickyard is. The place at present is only a little one horse affair, the brickyard will not develop it. It is a farming country, in fact one of the best in Ontario. We are told there will be a sawmill. It has been said that there was no timber there; perhaps that is rather a strong statement. I think nearly every farmer there has five or six acres of bush for his own use, that is all the timber there is for a saw mill. I may say to the minister that he will not be accused there of favouring the French people, because the French people there are as much opposed to this expenditure as anybody else. The French people in our part of the country are intelligent business men, and can easily see when money is being wasted. That French settlement I refer to is some ten miles long, and has been settled for forty or fifty years with French people from Lower Canada. I noticed this afternoon the minister, in referring to Bayfield, made comparisons. I do not object so much to the item for Bayfield, but the arguments that were brought forward to justify the present vote I think were very frivilous. He referred to the money spent in Bayfield thirty years ago. Well, those of us who knew that country thirty years ago know that there were no railroads when Bayfield harbour was built, and perhaps it was a proper expenditure. The grain in that portion of the country was all shipped from Bayfield, but to-day that Bayfield harbour is a dead letter. I am' not objecting to this vote, because the place may become a summer resort, it is growing in popularity ; but I am objecting to the argument advanced
by the minister for this vote when he refers to Bayfield, a work that has been useless for a number of years.

One would suppose from listening to the lion. Minister of Public Works that he was really indignant. Well now, he would have some right to be indignant if any person in this country were filching his pocket book the way he is filching the pocket book of the country. We have had two or three samples of that this session. This is only a small affair, he said; it is only a small amount that is involved. It is not a matter of principle with this hon, gentleman at all. It is merely a question of the amount that it is proposed to expend. If the hon. gentleman is hunting for places to put money tip for summer hotels, we can give him a job in the maritime provinces that will take him the rest of his life. If it has come to the point in this country that private enterprises are to be subsidized, as we have had. them subsidized during the last few years by the hon. Minister of Public Works, I think it is time that the public called a halt. Brickyards, saw mills, summer resorts 1 A similar case came up the other night and how admirably the hon. minister parried the point as to who owned the Lovell seigneury when it was proposed to give $53,000 to a private enterprise in Gaspe county. Last session we had some concessions made to the maritime provinces. They were going to make a magnificent harbour on a magnificent lake but when they made it the lake drained dry. That is how these hon. gentlemen are making themselves solid in the country perhaps, but are frittering away the money of the people. These private enterprises, I have no doubt, will take notice from the hon. minister's action this year, and probably next year Ottawa will hardly be able to hold the huge delegations that will be up to interview the minister and endeavour to persuade him to assist in their enterprises. Perhaps the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) could give us a good deal of information in regard to this particular matter. He is surely here to represent that constituency. If he is here I am certain the committee would be very much gratified to hear him explain the matter.

I think it is in one of Mar-ryatt's novels that a discussion arises as to what we will call an item in dispute and the excuse given, which, I think, was accepted, was that it was a very little one. I dare say there are many hon. members present who will remember what that refers to. This item in dispute is a very little one compared to most of the expenditures and items in dispute in this department. If we leave it, as the hon. minister suggests, I would say that it would facilitate the business of the committee to pass the whole estimates under this head, amounting to

$354,100, if the hon. minister will give ns his word that he will personally investigate each one of the works that it is proposed to expend this sum on in detail. It will take him a considerable time to do it, but if he will promise not to spend any money until he has first investigated all the items in this list, probably it would be better for us to pass them in a lump, taking the hon. minister's word that unless he finds there are brick-yards, town site exploiters or boomsters involved, or something that would justify the expenditure in each case, he will cancel the items and next year we will come here with a clean sheet and with no expenditure.

I understand the lion. Minister of Public 'Works to say that we are accusing him of a crime because he proposes to spend this money in this way. I did not think that any one on this side of the House went so far as that, but we do pretend to say that lie is committing a grave indiscretion. We do pretend to say that he is violating well understood principles of parliamentary government and asking the opposition to abandon the functions of an opposition, because he, himself, told us the other night that it was our duty, which we were expected to perform, to criticise every item according to the intelligence we possessed and the information we had, and to say whether it was right or wrong. We have accepted that invitation and we reply to him to-night that from our inquiry, our investigation and our information he is not justified in spending this money, nor are we justified in voting it. For that reason we oppose it. We also oppose it because we believe that a well understood principle of parliamentary government is that when a minister of the Crown asks the House to consider the advisability or otherwise of voting public money he is prepared to lay before it such information or data as he has acquired and collected with a statement to the House that will convince it that this expenditure should be made and therefore it will vote that it be made. But, he wants us to vote the money beforehand and give him a free hand to go and spend it after investigation if he likes, or to do the reverse. This is the most amusing proposition that I ever heard presented before this committee. It is the most Utopian proposition that I have ever heard presented to the committee for a long time. I am quite sure there is no hon. member of this committee who would more intensely oppose it than the hon. Mipister of Public Works himself if he were in opposition. I know the hon. gentleman too well not to believe that he would be the first man to condemn it. He would show up, not the iniquity exactly, but the impropriety of parliament voting public money on such a ground. The defence that it is a small item is no excuse whatever. It is the prin-
ciple involved in the matter ; it is not the amount of money involved.
What principle ?

The principle of asking parliament to vote money without having the data to justify it in voting that money. We are asking him for the verdict of his own friends but there is not a single hon. member of this House who will get up to say one word in defence of this proposition. The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) was in the House when this discussion commenced. Where is he now ? The hon. gentleman should tell the House what he thinks about it. He is not here to do it. He has found it convenient to get out of the House.
He is there.
Is he there ?
Yes.

If the hon. gentleman is present he should make a statement and let the committee know what he thinks about it. For these reasons we oppose it. If the hon. minister is prepared to give me his ear, I am prepared to go on with the discussion. We oppose it on another principle, and it is this : We think the principle of spending money on private property is wrong. It is not a government dock ; he told the committee that he does not know who owns the land, yet he makes that expenditure and after a while we will probably find out that we have to do as we have done in the past few years, when, after having spent money to enhance the value of private property we have been obliged to turn round and buy a dock for $10,000, or may be $20,000, the same as we had to do at Bruce Mines or in some other places. There is no public demand for this dock and there is no purpose in building it other than the booming of an imaginary townsite and the helping of a private individual to sell his land. That is the purpose. The brick yard business would be laughed at if you talked in tlie west about establishing a brick yard to export bricks to Chicago. And talk about building a harbour there. Why, only yesterday I happened to be in that section of the county, and met a gentleman who told me that he could roll up his pants and walk out twenty rods without wetting them. Yet the minister is going to give ten feet of water with an expenditure of $5,000. I have it on reliable authority that all that is moonshine. This gentleman whom I met said to me : The minister must have been very badly imposed upon; I admit that he is a man of a great deal of intelligence and if he was on the shore and looked at the exposed and shallow beach he would not require to be there fifteen seconds until he saw

the folly of trying to build a dock there to accommodate, what he says, are the needs of the country. The minister promises that he will go up and see that place, but what we object to is the principle of voting money upon such flimsy excuses. It is our duty here to vote away public money only when it is absolutely needed, and only when the minister convinces the House that there is sufficient trade in the locality to justify t(he expenditure.

The late John McMillan was a much respected member of this parliament. He was a farmer ; he was an old man and had been for twenty-five years a member of the House. In the month of May and in the month of Septembei', 1900, he transmitted to the department with his approval letters and petitions asking that a wharf be built there.
Perhaps if I ask the hon. minister how long it was before the general elections, it may explain the whole thing.

Well, that is a horse of another colour. I will not deviate from my argument. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) says that I have no ground to ask this parliament to vote this money, and I refer him to the authority of a member of parliament of twenty-five years' standing, who represented that riding, and who asked that a wharf should he built there. Of course, I take the full responsibility for what has been done in this matter, but I was away in 1900, and in my absence my colleagues ordered a survey and an examination. It was on the representation of a much-respected member of the Liberal party and of the House of Commons that this little enterprise was started. There were very great hopes then that a settlement would be made in that place. I have heard with surprise the statement of several members on the other side that there are no lands available for settlement there, because I understand that there is a large tract of land available and that already at least twenty-five families have settled there who were not there two years ago. We expected more. I repeat that a deputation of the Montreal business men and capitalists represented to me that they wanted to build a large hotel. The hotel has been started and there is the beginning of a settlement. What mistake have I committed in the face of all these statements ?

Will the hon. minister allow me to ask him if he is aware of the fact, that the very respectable member who recommended that and got him to put the item in the estimates, was defeated at the elecJ tions ? Will the minister also tell me, if he does not know that this very thing helped to defeat Mr. Macmillan ?

Without one word of opposition from the
ether side, this small amount was voted in the estimates, and on the faith of that vote I am told that a pretty large settlement has taken place there. All that I am asking is that the House shall not ask me to withdraw this amount from the estimates. I have not spent a dollar and I shall not spend a dollar until I have investigated the matter more fully. It is the privilege of gentlemen opposite to criticise this vote; and I have never complained of their criticism. I fully recognize the importance of being criticized, and I fully recognize the right of the opposition to do so. At the same time I believe that I am within my right and duty in insisting that the item should pass.
The minister told us that lie sent an engineer to get a report on this work. Will he be good enough to place that report on the Table ?
If my hon. friend moves for that report he will get it with pleasure.

The Minister of Public Works seems anxious to avoid the peculiar position he has placed himself in. He tells us that he will not expend this money until he inquires whether the expenditure is justifiable or not. I misunderstand the duties of a minister, responsible to this parliament and under a responsible government, if such a plea should prevail. The hon. gentleman must see the ridiculous position he is in. He asks the House to have perfect confidence in him; he tells us that he may not make the expenditure, but he wants us to vote a sum of money without his being able to justify the expenditure. What an extraordinary and absurd position ? I venture to say that such an exhibition was never made by a minister before. Under responsible government, the minister cannot ask a vote from this House without first being convinced himself of the absolute necessity of the expenditure; then he must convince his colleagues that the vote should be submitted to the House, and then he must have the approval of the Governor General on the ground that the expenditure is in the public interest. But the minister now asks us that the money shall be granted to him in trust, and he pledges his honour to the House that if the expenditure is not justifiable he will not make it. Why do we not vote all appropriations in the same manner ? Why do we not give a lump sum to the minister and trust to his honour and judgment as to the expediency of the expenditure ? That is not our form of government at all; that is not ministerial responsibility. That is the position of the Minister of Public Works.
It is not the position.

It is exactly the position of the Minister of Public Works. A more absurd and ridiculous position a

minister never occupied in this House at all. Why does he not come out manfully and say, I am responsible for the expenditure, and I ask this House to vote the money, instead of asking us to trust to his honour and his knowledge and experience, to decide whether the expenditure is justifiable or not. X will venture to say that such a request was never presented to a constitutional assembly before this evening.

What is the use of my hon. friend trying to lecture me on constitutional law, which I know just as well as he does, if not better ? The amount was placed in the estimates when my hon. friend was in the House, and lie did not object to it or say one word against it. If it were a new vote altogether, my position would not be as clear as it is; but it is not a new vote: the amount has been in the estimates for years, and I simply ask that it be allowed to remain there until I get further information. My hon. friend's lecture is not in the right direction. I do not profess to be infallible on constitutional law, but in this case I do not believe I am making a mistake, in taking the position that this amount having been placed in the estimates, I do not want to withdraw it without more information. I think that is a fair position, and if our lion, friends opposite cannot agree with us, I am very sorry.

It seems to me that the minister has not improved his position at all. He says this is partly a revote. That shows that he has had a year or two to ascertain whether it is a proper vote or not; but he does not know now any more than he did twelve months ago whether there is any necessity for a harbour at this place. That being the case, there is no need of putting this vote through to-night, and it may continue to rest in the imagination of the hon. minister without doing any harm to anybody. I do not think the minister's statement that it was voted before is any reason why he should revote it. Surely when it comes before parliament it is a new vote, and should be considered without regard to the past, if the work has not been commenced. Evidently it is a useless expenditure, or the minister would be able to give some reason why the money was not expended. The opposition know more of the matter now than they did when the item was in the estimates last year, and they know that it is one that should not pass the House.

Our friends on the other side have been so exceedingly good to the hon. Minister of Public Works in allowing so many items to pass that they appear to have arranged a little tilt to-night in order to have a little amusement I am not familar with this particular work. I Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
have obtained my information of it from what has been said to-night by the hon. Minister of Public Works and the hon. gentlemen on the other side; and if I were on the other side, animated with a desire to make a little political capital out of this matter, I could convince myself that our friends over there are probably adopting the right course; but if we look at it as a business proposition, I think the attitude of the minister is quite reasonable. He says that on the representations of an influential committee of gentlemen from Montreal, and also at the request of a number of people who live in the district, and under the advice of the late Mr. McMillan, a gentleman whom we all respected, he was induced to place a sum in the estimates for this work. This year renewed pressure was brought upon him to go on with this work, and in good faith he puts the item in the estimates. He is not to suppose that conditions have changed; he expects that the matter will be treated as a business proposition; and for the first time he hears objections to the scheme which he was not aware of before. He is not satisfied, however, and I am not satisfied, that all the statements made on the other side of the House are correct. We hear so many statements emanating from that source that on subsequent investigation we find to be inaccurate that we feel quite justified sometimes in taking Ijhe statements that are made by our hon. friends opposite with a little grain of suspicion. I am on this occasion with the minister. I say that he was justified, upon the information he had, in putting this item in the estimates, and he is not willing to withdraw it upon the statements made by our friends on the other side. But at the same time they have created enough suspicion in his mind to induce him to satisfy himself as to their accuracy, and if he finds them to be true, he is willing that this particular sum shall not be expended. That is quite sufficient for me as a supporter of the hon. minister, and I am quite willing, if the opposition insist on that item standing, to support the minister with my vote. I have learned, after four or five years experience in this House, not to believe everything that emanates from the other side of the Speaker.

The hon. gentleman who has just sat down is no doubt very much in touch with the Minister of Public Works, because the Minister of Public Works announces himself to be an out-and-out protectionist; and in these days, when my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) is losing so much sleep looking after the interests of his political sponsors, the Massey-Harris Company, and asking for additional protection for them, I can readily understand why he rushes to the help of the Minister of Public Works.
That is not in his department.

No, but my hon. friend from South Brant will acknowledge the great prestige and power which the hon. Minister of Public Works possesses in the Cabinet. Now, what is the first statement made by the hon. member for South "Brant to justify his position ? He says that a deputation from Montreal waited on the Minister of Public Works and asked that this work be proceeded with. Now, who were the gentlemen who waited on the Minister of Public Works ? It was a gentleman who was building a summer hotel, and wanted a dock to lead up to it. Surely my hon. friend does not contend that the money of this country should be used to build docks for people who wish to build summer hotels? My hon. friend from South Brant poses as a business man in this House, and yet he stands op and says that if a gentleman desires to build a summer hotel at any point in the Dominion, all he needs to do, in his opinion, is to apply to the people of this country for a wharf to be built at the public expense, to be used in conjunction with his hotel. I am surprised that my hon. friend is not asking the Minister of Public Works to build a livery stable for some gentleman who wishes to start one and hire out horses. Surely, if it is right to build a wharf to accommodate a man who is building a summer hotel, it is equally right to build a livery stable for any one who wants to engage in that business. Now, there are two principles involved in this matter, and it is immaterial whether the vote is $5,000 or $50,000. What did we have in this House the other night ? The Minister of Public Works made the statement that the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell), having a large timber tract in the county of Gaspfi, desired to establish mills there, and in order to save expenditure in connection with his mill, he wanted the government of the country, or the people-because it is the people's money-to build a $50,000 dock for him. Nobody disputed that that was the case, and the hon. gentleman stated that the building of a saw-mill was contingent on the government building the dock. The hon. member for South Brant, if in the House, I presume, acquiesced in that. The hon. gentleman now attacks the statements made by my hon. friend from North Middlesex (Mr. Sherritt). I think he is very unfair to my hon. friend, who does not obtrude himself very much on the House; and when he makes statements of fact in this House, living as he does a few miles from the place, it is bad grace on the part of the hon. member for South Brant to suggest that those statements are not true. I will be bound to say that every statement the hon. member for North Middlesex makes is true.
The gentleman who represents the riding where this wrork is to be done left the chamber as soon as it was mentioned. That cannot be denied. He was sitting in the House immediately before this item was called and then left the chamber. Why did he leave ? Because he knew he could not make any statement of facts that would at all justify it. The statement of the Minister of Public Works itself makes out a case, which could not be possibly stronger, for any one attacking this expenditure. He said that the demand for this work came first from a gentleman who owned the land, that this gentleman intended constructing a summer hotel at that point, and that there is a saw-mill there. No one denies these facts, but the mill has no connection with the dock because it is not even built on the water's edge. It is a small mill intended to cut up logs that are now standing timber in that part of the country. It is not built near the water edge at all. Then as regards the brickyard, it is absurd to talk of building a dock in order that brick may be exported to the United States. Every one knows that brick is not exported to the United States from this country. But in order to get this vote through, the minister makes this novel pledge, which has been commented on by my hon. friends from North Lanark (Mr. I-Iaggart) and West Toronto (Mr. Osier). He gives the House his word that if on inquiry he finds that the circumstances do not justify the expenditure, the money will not be spent. Well, he need not have waited to make a personal visit for he could have got all the information he required from the hon. member in whose riding this work is to be done. And the fact that that hon. gentleman deliberately went out of the chamber as soon as the item was called is pretty clear evidence that there is no justification for it. Or the hon. minister could have called on Mr. Deputy Speaker, who might have left the Chair, and attempted some justification of this vote. But neither of these two gentlemen ventured to defend it.
I was surprised to find the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) rising to support this vote. I thought at first that this was the last straw breaking the camel's back, and that the hon. gentleman was really rising in his place in protest. Then there is the hon. member for South Perth, who went out against the government on the Yukon deal. That was a question of principle with the hon. gentleman. Is he going to stulify the reputation for independence which he made on that occasion ? Is he going to sit here and vote for a proposition, which the minister himself says he is not now in a position to justify. Is he going to vote for expenditure on a work which is of no public utility at all, but which, as the Minister of Public of Works has himself
