said, was taken up by the government on the request of a private individual, who asked to have his private property improved at the expense of the public.

I have seen a good many tempests in a teapot, but this is the smallest kind of a tempest and the smallest kind of a pot I ever saw. Whether the hon. gentleman who represents one of the Hurons is or is not in the House or whether our Chairman did not leave the Chair in order to address the House, does not affect the case. Why should the Minister of Public Works or of any other department withdraw an item at the dictation of the opposition ? This item was placed in the estimates, with the consent of the House, and because two or three of my hon. friends on the other side have thought proper to rise in their might and tell me that I am not to be trusted with this wonderful sum of money, I am forsooth to drop the item. They threaten us with a vote. Well, if we have nothing more to fear than a division on a question like this, we will be very long on this side of the House. I repeat that this item was placed in the estimates with the consent of hon. gentlemen opposite. Circumstances justified the government in placing it in the estimates, and because I do not now eat humble pie, because I do not make up my mind to be lectured by my hon. friend's opposite, we are going to have a vote. We have had votes in the past and have not been killed by them, and I do not think we stand much danger of being slaughtered on this occasion. We will see whether the country will support hon. gentlemen opposite in their demands that I should withdraw this item without being given the chance of looking into it myself. This is a most unreasonable position for the opposition to take. I hope that my hon. friends have no other motive than to vindicate constitutional law, and the country will judge whether it is any such high motive which animates them on this occasion. I have nothing more to add except to call the attention of my hon. friend who has just sat down, to the unfairness of his statement. I do not suppose that he meant to be unfair but what is the use of his saying that the sum was placed in the estimates at the exclusive demand of gentlemen from Montreal.
I understood the hon. minister to say that Mr. Cantin and another gentleman had asked for the grant in the first instance.

We have devoted a good deal of time to this item, and if we are to take a vote, we might as well take it now. I do not think anything more can be said which would throw any additional light on this subject. The position Mr. BENNETT.
is this. A couple of years ago a sum was placed in the estimates for the building of a wharf at the place in question. There was some business representations made to my hon. colleague, the Minister of Public Works, on behalf of this expenditure, and he acceded. This appears this year to have shocked the sense of my hon. friend from Simcoe in particular among others. But he ought not to be so very particular. Why, this very afternoon he asked the hon. Minister of Public Works to put an item in the estimates of $3,000 for an expenditure at Orillia, and for no other reason than that the Minister of Public Works had paid a visit to Orillia last summer, and that on that occasion my hon. friend had brought all the pretty girls of that town in a deputation to ask him to have a wharf built there. There were no business reasons, but simply this appeal to my hon. colleague who, having French blood in his veins, is very susceptible and could not resist the blandishments of the fair sex of that charming little town. But my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) and the opposition had no fault to find with my hon. colleague for his susceptibility on that occasion. On the contrary they invited the Minister of Public Works to accede to that appeal of the fair maidens of Orillia. I do not think therefore that it lies in the mouth of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) to blame the Minister of Public Works for following this precedent.

The tenor of the hon. minister's defence is simply this, that the item was put in last year and the opposition did not object. But at the time there did not happen to be among hon. members on this side any one who kney the locality well enough to express an intelligent opinion on the expenditure, and we accepted it on the strength of the statement of the Minister of Public Works that it was needed. But, this year, we tell him we have the information and that he is not justified in asking for this vote. The only defence he has is that we did not object last year. It may have been wrong, he tells us, but the fact that we did it last year is the reason why we should do it this year.
It is a reason for looking into the matter.

Two wrongs do not make a right. Though, for want of information, we let it pass last year, yet now that we have acquired information we tell him it is wrong. That is a reason why he should refrain from pushing it. He said that an hon. member in this House, who is not now in the House, recommended this vote. And that gentleman went to the country two months afterwards and was defeated. That was not a very strong argument in favour of the expenditure. The hon. gentleman

says that he sent an engineer and got a report. If that report justifies the expenditure, why not give it to the House and convince the House that the money should be voted ? The hon. gentleman keeps back the report and tells us to move for it, and it will be brought down. That is, vote the money first and see the report afterwards. We want that report now, so that we may know whether it justifies us in voting this money or not. The very fact that he says he will not spend a dollar of this mofiey until he sends another engineer to report discredits the engineer he sent in the first place.	-

The Minister of Public Works tells us that he was recommended by the late member for the county to build the dock. He laid great stress upon that. I would ask him if he has asked the opinion of the hon. gentleman now representing the county ?
I did not.
Does not the hon. gentleman think that the hon. member who now represents the county, now that this thing has been noised abroad, would be able to give valuable suggestions ?

The hon. gentleman who represents the county never asked me to withdraw the item. I will act in this case as I acted in the Presqu'Isle case. I looked into that matter carefully, and this year I asked to withdraw the vote. If, on investigating this matter, I find that I have been misinformed, I will do what I did in the Presqu'Isle case. More than that, I must not be asked to; more than that, I will not do.
Has the present member for the county never made any suggestion on the point ?
No.
If I do not mistake, I see the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McCreary) standing in the entrance to this chamber. Perhaps he will come in and give his opinion upon this matter.

We have heard from the minister several times that we are as much responsible as are the occupants of the government benches for some of these items. I can only say that if the minister will be frank with us when he attempts to fly his kite, we will acknowledge our responsibility. But a case arose the other night. Last year he had flown a small kite of $15,000; this year he comes with the tail to the kite in the form of an additional $38,000. If the minister wants us to be responsible, let him give us the absolute facts when these items come before us, so that we may know whether we are going to spend $5,000 or $100,000. A vote of $15,000 last year hardly justified him in making a contract for $53,000. But that is what he did. Then he comes to us and says I have thrown this little sop to a supporter of the government, and we want you to ladle out the rest of the money so as to keep this gentleman quiet. The sooner the members of the opposition and the people of the country generally understand this system, the better it will be for all. The hon. minister has been remarkably considerate of one of his friends in the cabinet, the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock). You will remember that the Postmaster General issued a circular, and not only that, but he issued it when the hon. Minister of Public Works was in Europe. This is one of these ill-omened birds that sometimes come home to roost. I. have no doubt that the minister has on file the application for this vote. Probably those who made it gave as one of their reasons for making it this circular of the Postmaster General. Perhaps there are other applications of a similar nature on file, and it might be well for the minister to bring them down. It would be interesting to know how many applications have arisen from that circular of the Postmaster General. That circular probably had about as much good effect as the Labour Bureau that we are paying for. The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) gave a wonderful justification of this vote. That justification was that the hon. member said so, and that was enough. The Postmaster General's circular led to the asking for it, the Minister of Public. Works granted it, and the hon. member for South Brant is willing to support it. There has been a considerable exhibition this evening of a sort of weakness of the knees. I have noticed it several times in the case of the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). He was in a back seat and he partly rose, but dropped back again- his heart failed him. He has come down a seat or two and has tried to get on his feet. I hope he will have strength enough to get up and either defend this vote, or do as he ought to do, move that it would be struck out.
It is not in my riding.

I think we need no further evidence than the refusal of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) to see that this item is not a good one. I wish to point out the dangerous character of the doctrine laid down by the Minister of Public Works when he says that the opposition, by consenting to this item last year, gave up their right to object to it this year. If that is followed up to its logical conclusion, then, every new item that is placed in the estimates should be objected to by the opposition whether they have any knowledge in the

matter or not, whether they believe the item to be reasonable or not. As a member of the opposition, I object to taking that stand. I do not think it would be in the interest of the country or in the interest of the members of this House. The course the opposition is taking on this occasion is, in my judgment, the only proper course to take, namely, that if they know of no reasonable objection to an item, then the item should be allowed to pass the House. But if they find there are objections to an item, then they would be neglectful of their duty if they did not rise and object to it. I want to tell the Minister of Public Works that so far as I am concerned, I care not when an item appears in the estimates, if it is ten years hence, and I should be then a member of this House, and it was again submitted to the House, I would take the opportunity of rising in my place and objecting to it.

I wish to say a few words with reference to the statement of the Minister of Public Works as to a duty of the opposition in criticising items which appear in the estimates. I would not have paid much attention to it were it not that I notice that the same argument was used by the Minister of Finance when addressing the electors in one of the Ontario constituencies. He argued that because the opposition had not challenged an item in the estimates by their vote, that therefore they consented to it. A more absurd statement was never made by any minister. Let the Minister of Public Works read the statement of the hon. Joseph Chamberlain when he was criticised in the same direction. He said the government was responsible for every item that was put in the estimates, and that the duty of the opposition was confined to fair criticism. Their duty is, not to divide the House upon an estimate they object to, but to state their objections and leave it there. And yet we are told by the Minister of Finance of this country that because the opposition did not divide the House on an estimate, therefore they consented to it. Let him read the speech of Mr. Chamberlain where he shows the absurdity of such an argument, let him read the speeches of leading statesmen in England on the same subject, and he will find that they hold the principle that the duty of an opposition is merely criticism, not to divide the House on an item, but to leave the entire responsibility with the government who propose it. If we do not divide the House upon it, that is no reason why we should be accused of supporting the vote. The Prime Minister says we may as well have a division at once upon the subject. Let me answer that we do not divide the House in committee where the votes are not registered.
One of the hon. gentleman's friends has just moved to have the vote struck out.
I have not heard anything of the kind.
The member for Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) just moved it.
No.
I beg his pardon then, I misunderstood him.

We do not divide the House where the votes are not registered, as it would be useless to do so. Our opposition is not so much for the purpose of influencing the government as for the purpose of influencing the country, because we know we are in a minority in this House, and when we divide the House we want our votes to appear to the public throughout the Dominion to show whether we support an item or not. The Minister of Public Works taunts the opposition with having made no objection to the vote last year. The position we ocupy as a party is that for every item in the estimates the government of the day are responsible, and that our functions are confined to criticising an item we object to. That is the principle laid down by English statesmen, as I have just mentioned.

I fully agree with the constitutional views which the hon. member for Lanark has just expressed. Let the hon. gentleman understand me well. I stated that last year there was no opposition to this item, but in saying that I did not mean to argue that our friends opposite have no right to oppose the item this year. But I say that having raised no opposition last year, it is too late for them to expect that I will withdraw the item now when, for the first time they raise an opposition.
You have not spent a dollar yet.

Let our friends opposite understand me well. They did not oppose this item last year, and they have not since then shown sufficient reason to induce me to withdraw it this year. I quite understand that the opposition have every right to criticise the items in the estimates, whether they were placed there last year or this year. When the Minister of Finance argued in the country that the opposition consented to votes by not dividing the House upon them, he meant to convey the idea, which is a true one, that the opposition are every day asking us to spend money for public works in their ridings' still, when they discuss the Budget, either in the House or in the country, they complain that we are spending too much. I claim that they are not fair, and that the Minister of Finance was perfectly right in saying what he did.
I am perfectly satisfied that if the minister will go down and look

over this place as lie has promised to do, he will be convinced that the proposed expenditure is not a proper one to make. I understood him to say there was a lot of land available that could be got for settlers. That is true in a sense, but the country is an old settled country. I think land there is worth $40 an acre. There Is no wild land there available for settlers. I wish the Chairman was in a position to rise and give us his opinion upon this proposition. The country has been settled ever since I was a boy. The farmers own, perhaps, five or six acres of timber each. I am perfectly satisfied that if the minister goes down there and examines the situation he will be convinced that he has been misled, and he will not spend this money, because I think the hon. gentleman will not break faith with the House nor go back on his promise. I wish to say now, in answer to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd), that I think he was a little too harsh in accusing me of making statements that are not absolutely correct. I feel that my actions in the House do not justify him in making such a statement as that about me. I have not taken up very much of the time of the House.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sherritt) (thinks that I made a reflection upon anything he said, I can assure him that such was very far from my intention. I have not the slightest doubt but that everything he said was true in connection with this matter.

I am glad to accept that apology, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that I am in a position to know a little of what I am talking about. There are some questions in reference to this matter, particularly as to the number of people there, that I do not feel inclined to answer, but I make this statement that a few years ago this locality was an open field used for farming purposes. A gentleman came there and started a summer hotel, and commenced the erection of some other buildings. There are a number of proposed buildings with northing but the foundations completed. This gentleman undertook to make a city, but he failed in that effort and the hotel stands there to-day unfinished. There is no business man in that part of the country but considers that the time is coming when the hotel will be torn down and the brick used for the erection of bank barns. It is an agricultural country. There is noit a tree near the place to provide the shade necessary for a summer resort. It has been suggested that this gentleman is going to bring trees there and make a grove. This man has failed to do as he contemplated, and he comes with a deputation to the minister. I know if the hon. minister goes down there and examines the place for himself he will return to this
House and say that he will not go on with this expenditure. The late Mr. McMillan has been referred to, a gentleman that I knew for many years, and one in whom I have had every confidence. If it is in accordance with .the rules of the House, * I would like the hon. Minister of Public Works to bring down the letter which he says he received from the late Mr. McMillau and show it to the House because, having every confidence in the late Mr. McMillan, I cannot believe that he ever considered this a proper place in which to spend money for the making of a harbour. I hope, if it is not contrary to the rules of the House, the hon. minister will have that letter brought down that we may have an opportunity of reading it.
Toronto hi.rbour-works at eastern entrance, &c., $8,000.

The vote in the estimates for Toronto harbour is rather infinitesimal when we consider the amount we have just been discussing. We have had a vote of $5,000 for a village supposed to contain twenty-five families. Estimating that each of these families contains ten members apiece that would be 250 people, the proportionate vote would be about $5,000,000 for Toronto containing about 250,000 people. While 1 am a strong objector to spending public money except judiciously, and where it will result for the general good of the community, I do think that the amount the hon. Minister of Public Works and the government have been devoting to the most important harbour in Canada, practically, a harbour where there has been more business done than in any other harbour in the Dominion, is so absurd that there can be only one explanation for it and this explanation appears to be, that, do what they can, the government cannot get supporters of their own returned for Toronto. Perhaps it is unfortunate that Toronto should be such a Conservative city, but the fact remains that practically no public money is being expended on the most important harbour in Canada. I agree, I must say, with the position that the hon. Minister of Public Works has taken in connection with the main expenditure on the harbour that the government should not expend money there until the city of Toronto takes charge of its own drainage. I agree with the hon. minister there entirely. In regard to the question of the straightening of the Don, or preventing the silt which comes down from the Don and is filling up the harbour, it is entirely another matter, and it is one which should be taken charge of by the government. The government should take charge of the silt which comes down from that river and should prevent the harbour from being filled up as it has been with this silt. The money that is voted for the improvement of Toronto harbour is simply absurd.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) will allow me, I will not enter Into a discussion of the question from the standpoint that he has just adopted. This small amount of money is applied for to pay the balance of the contract which is going on. I must have the money to pay it and to erect three groynes that were asked from me the last time I had the pleasure of being in Toronto. As to the larger question it will bt* discussed in the supplementary estimates. The main estimates contain nothing at all for new works.
All right.
There will be an appropriation in the supplementary estimates for the diversion of the Don river ?

When the supplementary estimates come down my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) will find whether there is an amount or not. I am not free to say now. I have never given any definite answer to any member of parliament no matter to which side he might belong. The supplementary estimates have not yet been decided upon.

The hour is late, and I do not wish to have the discussion just now, but I want to let the hon. minister know that on the supplementary estimates we desire to have a full discussion of the Toronto harbour and the diversion of the Don.
There will be no trouble about that.

On this question of the supplementary estimates, I wish to say a word or two in regard to this particular vote. It seems to me very objectionable that estimates should be brought down piecemeal when the minister knows there are going to be supplementary estimates. I think that when a supplementary estimate is intended by the minister the main vote should be postponed until the supplementary estimate is brought down.
It has never been done in that way here.

It may not have been. I do not understand how a body of men can intelligently decide upon whether they will vote any sum whatever when they know a further sum is going to be asked for. The fact that a further sum is likely to be asked for might influence the minds of hon. gentlemen as to whether they would grant any sum at all.
Manitoba-general repairs and improvements to harbour, river and bridge works, $3,000.
This is the usual vote.

I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he has done anything since last session to improve the mouth of the Mossey river ? He will remember that last session I drew his attention to the fact that there was a bar across the mouth of that river, and that he promised to send an officer to look into the matter. He had a dredge on Lake Manitoba and he proposed to send it up there to do this work.

The chief engineer tells me that he has instructed our resident engineer in Manitoba to make a survey, but he is not sure whether he has received his report or hot. We will look into the question, if my hon. friend (Mr. Roche) will be good enough to call at the office we will show him the report if it is there.
Where is this particular vote to be expended ?

It is a general vote to be expended all over the province.
Columbia river-improvomimts in1 narrows between upper and lower Arrow lakes, $10,000.
What improvements do you intend to make there ?
We have given a contract for a small dredge to carry on the improvements.
Is this for a dredge ?
Yes.
Then, the wording of your item is wrong. It speaks of the improvements in the channel.
The best way of making these improvements is to build a dredge there.
Then you should ask for money to build the dredge. The wording of the item is misleading. I do not think the minister will try to justify that.

I believe it is all right. We are doing the same thing at Lake Temiscamingue. Suppose instead of building a dredge I should buy shovels and things like that to make the improvements. I think I am justified in getting the dredge.

The minister may be quite justified in building a dredge, but he cannot take the money for that purpose from a vote to improve the channel. The Auditor General would not allow that to pass if he was looking after it, because one of his duties is to see that the money voted by

parliament for a specific purpose is spent for that purpose.
I think it is all right. I do not hide anything, I am stating the facts.
I do not say that you are not stating the facts, but I complain of the impropriety of voting money for one purpose and spending it on another.
I have no objection to changing the wording of the item if the hon. gentleman wishes. I move to add the words ' to include the building of a dredge.'

That is all right then.
Item, as amended, agreed to.
